lessons.title: A world inside a cell

lead.text: We begin outside, at the surface of one cell. Whatever its shape, a cell is a small bag of watery living material, and the bag is never shut off from the world. Food and oxygen have to get in, and waste has to get out, all day long.

Something in the skin of the bag has to decide what goes where. A skin that sealed the cell would starve it and trap its own waste. A skin with no control at all would let the contents drift out and the cell's chemistry fall apart. Every cell has a thin layer that sits between those extremes, called the plasma membrane or cell membrane. It acts like a doorkeeper, letting some substances through and holding others back.

afterFigure.text: The two cells in the picture look quite different inside, yet both are wrapped in a plasma membrane. So is every other living cell. Everything we meet from here on lies inside it. The first thing to find there is the cell's store of instructions.

lead.text: Think back to the edge of the animal cell and of the bacterium.

Inside the membrane, the first thing to find is the cell's instructions. Every cell carries a complete set, written in a long molecule called DNA, and it uses them to build its parts and to make copies of itself. Where a cell keeps that molecule is the clearest way to tell one kind of cell from another.

Animal cells and plant cells are eukaryotic (say yoo-KARR-ee-OT-ik). In a eukaryotic cell most of the DNA sits inside a nucleus, a compartment with a membrane of its own. A good picture is a locked office in the middle of a busy workshop. The master plans stay safe in one place, away from the noise and the chemistry going on outside. Use the Inspect menu under the picture to find the nucleus of the animal cell.

afterFigure.text: Now switch to the bacterium and choose Nucleoid from the menu. A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane round it, more like plans pinned to the wall of one open room. The DNA does the same job, and it simply isn't shut away.

So you can sort cells into two kinds by looking at where the DNA sits. If it sits behind a membrane of its own, in a nucleus, the cell is eukaryotic. If it lies in a nucleoid, the cell is a bacterium. Eukaryotic cells also contain other compartments, and those are the next stop.

lead.text: A bacterium still has instructions to store, but it has no compartment to store them in.

steps.headline: The working parts of a eukaryotic cell

lead.text: The nucleus is only one of several parts packed into a eukaryotic cell, and the parts are not interchangeable. Each is built for one job, and a part like that is called an organelle, which means 'little organ'. A cell works rather like a workshop with separate rooms, each set up for one task.

The first room to know is the power station. Mitochondria (one is a mitochondrion) take the energy stored in fuel such as sugar and hand it over in a form the cell can spend. A cell that spends a lot of energy, like a muscle cell, is packed with them. Pick Mitochondria from the Inspect menu to see where they sit.

afterFigure.text: Then there are the ribosomes, tiny benches where the cell builds proteins by following instructions copied from its DNA. Proteins are the molecules that do most of the cell's work, from building its parts to speeding up its chemistry. Ribosomes are so basic that bacteria have them too. A bacterium has no mitochondria, though, because it has no compartments with membranes of their own.
An animal cell has all of these. A leaf cell has one more organelle, and that is the next stop.

lead.text: Now move from the animal cell to a leaf. A leaf cell has everything the animal cell has, plus chloroplasts. A chloroplast is an organelle that catches light energy, and it holds the green colouring that makes leaves green. The cell uses the energy it catches to make sugar. Choose Chloroplasts from the Inspect menu on the leaf cell, then switch to the animal cell and look for them there.

afterFigure.text: Chloroplasts need light to work, and light does not reach every part of a plant. A cell in a root lives in dark soil and has none. It stays alive on sugar made in the leaves and sent down to it, and it still has mitochondria to release the energy from that sugar.
A leaf cell carries two organelles that deal with energy. One catches light and the other works on fuel. That raises a puzzle about what the cell does when the light goes out.

lead.text: Night falls over the leaf, and no light reaches its cells.

That completes the tour inside, so the last stop is back at the surface of the leaf cell. Outside its plasma membrane a plant cell has one more layer, the cell wall. It is a stiff, tough shell. Think of a water balloon sitting inside a cardboard box: the balloon can swell only until it presses against the box. Choose Cell wall from the menu to see it.

afterFigure.text: The wall is full of gaps, so water and dissolved substances pass through it easily. It gives the cell a fixed shape, and it leaves the control of what enters and leaves to the plasma membrane inside it.

Plant cells are not the only ones that build a wall. Most bacteria have one as well, although the bacterium drawn earlier leaves it out to keep the picture simple. A wall by itself doesn't show that a cell is eukaryotic, whereas a nucleus does.

lead.text: Plants have no skeleton, yet a leaf stands up.

blocks.text: A drop of pond water under a microscope is crowded. Specks drift and swim through it, and some of them are green. Many of the specks are single cells, and each one is alive in the same ways you are. It takes in food and gets rid of waste, and it carries a complete set of instructions for building more of itself.

All of that happens inside a bag far too small to see. Dozens of animal cells would fit side by side across the head of a pin, and a bacterium is smaller still. Yet the bag has structure. Its edge controls what comes and goes, and inside it the parts have separate jobs, a little like a workshop with a locked office and a row of benches.
This lesson goes inside. We start at the cell's edge and move inwards one stop at a time. Each stop is a part with a job, and the parts we find let us tell one kind of cell from another.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a bacterium from an animal or plant cell, and say what each main part is for.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in biology happens inside these cells.

recap.keyIdea: Every cell has a plasma membrane. Eukaryotic cells also have a nucleus and organelles with jobs, while a bacterium keeps its DNA in a nucleoid.

blocks.text: Back at the drop of pond water, each speck now has parts you can name. You named the plasma membrane every cell shares, worked out where a bacterium keeps its DNA, and decided which organelle keeps a leaf cell going after dark.

recap.nextHook: Everything a cell takes in or lets out has to cross its membrane, and the next lesson starts with two rooms and an open door to show which way a crowd of particles drifts.

lessons.title: Which way will molecules move?

steps.headline: Two rooms and an open door

lead.text: Look at the rooms a little more closely. Everyone wanders at random, but the doorway is the same for everybody, so the number who cross in each direction depends only on how many people are in each room. Suppose that in each minute a quarter of the people in a room happen to go through the door.

In the first minute a quarter of the 20 people on the left (5 people) cross to the right, while a quarter of the 4 people on the right (1 person) crosses to the left. Five go one way and one goes the other, so the difference between the two crossings is 4 people. That difference is the net movement: 4 people from left to right. The rooms now hold 16 and 8.

The second minute works the same way. A quarter of 16 is 4 and a quarter of 8 is 2, so the net movement falls to 2 people and the rooms hold 14 and 10. Each minute the net movement is half what it was, because the gap between the rooms is half what it was.

Nobody pushes the crowd out of the full room. It drifts because a crowded room has more people to send through the door than a sparse one, and the closer the rooms get to equal numbers, the slower the drift becomes. The same counting works for anything that moves at random, which includes the particles in a cell.
Back to the rooms as they began, with a crowd wandering at random through an open door.

Now swap the people for particles. When sugar or a dye dissolves in water it breaks up into separate particles. The dissolved substance is called a solute. Water molecules are always jostling the solute particles, so each one wanders at random, just like a person in the rooms.

Replace the rooms with two compartments of equal size and the doorway with a membrane that lets the solute through, and the same counting applies. The word for how crowded a solute is in a given space is its concentration. Because the compartments are the same size, the side with more particles is the side with the higher concentration.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider under the picture. The particles drift towards equal numbers on the two sides, and the movement slows as they level out. This net movement of a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated is called diffusion. Either side can be the more concentrated one, so the direction comes from comparing the two.
With the direction settled, the next thing to find out is how far the movement goes before it stops.

lead.text: Apply the rule to a new pair of compartments, equal in size.

The net movement stops when the two sides are equally concentrated. With compartments of the same size, that happens when they hold the same amount, and a state where the net movement has stopped is called equilibrium.

To find the equal amount, remember that diffusion only moves particles from one side to the other. None is made and none is lost, so the total on the two sides stays fixed. Add the two sides together, then split the total evenly.
Take 9 units on one side and 3 on the other. The total is 12, so at equilibrium each side holds 6. The crowded side falls from 9 to 6, so 3 units must cross.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider in each case. The second one also has a total of 12, so it settles at 6 on each side too, and this time the right side is the crowded one that loses units.

lead.text: Add the two sides, then share the total between the equal volumes.

Return to the two rooms once they hold 12 people each. A visitor looking in would see no change, because the counts stay put. The wandering has not stopped, though. A quarter of each room, which is 3 people, still goes through the door every minute, in each direction.

The traffic through the door is as busy as ever, but the two crossings are equal and cancel out. That is what equilibrium means: the net movement is zero while the people, or the particles, go on moving. In the compartments, individual particles keep crossing both ways at the same rate, and the amount on each side stays the same. In the picture the first case is at equilibrium and the second is not.

afterFigure.text: This matters to a living cell. A cell that keeps using up the oxygen reaching it holds less oxygen per unit of space than its surroundings, so the net movement never falls to zero. Oxygen keeps arriving through the membrane, and the cell spends no effort bringing it in.

lead.text: Two compartments of equal size have reached equilibrium, and solute is still crossing between them.

Everything so far assumed that the solute could cross. A real membrane has a say in that, as the doorkeeper from the first lesson does. A membrane is permeable to a substance if that substance can cross it, and impermeable to it if it cannot.
Those words describe a membrane's behaviour towards one substance at a time. The same membrane can be permeable to water and impermeable to a dye.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two cases and move the slider in each. When the solute can cross, the sides level out. When it cannot, each side keeps the amount it started with, no matter how different they are, because nothing crosses to change them. A difference in concentration produces movement only when the substance can get through.
So the first question to ask about any membrane is what can cross it. Water often can when a solute cannot, and the next lesson follows what happens then.

lead.text: Now take away every route across the barrier.

blocks.text: A cell trades with the world around it all day. Food and oxygen come in and waste goes out, and every item has to cross the membrane we met in the last lesson. For much of this traffic the cell does no pushing at all, yet the goods still move in a steady direction.

The pattern is easiest to see at a bigger scale. Picture two rooms of equal size joined by an open doorway. At the start 20 people stand in the left room and 4 in the right. Everyone wanders about at random, and nobody has been told which way to go.

After a while the numbers in the two rooms will have changed, and the way they change follows a rule that particles in water obey as well. This lesson finds that rule, then puts a membrane in the doorway and sees what changes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way a dissolved substance moves across a membrane, and when it will not move at all.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains how cells take in nutrients without spending energy.

recap.keyIdea: A solute that can cross a membrane moves net from the crowded side to the sparse side until the concentrations match. A solute that cannot cross stays put.

blocks.text: You followed 24 people to equal numbers in two rooms, shared units of solute between equal compartments, and saw that a solute the membrane blocks keeps its starting amount. Back at the doorway, you can now say which way a crowd of particles drifts and when it stops.

recap.nextHook: A membrane can pass water and stop a solute, and the next lesson asks what happens to the water when it does.

lessons.title: When only water can cross

lead.text: Start with a cup of squash. Two spoonfuls of syrup stirred into a litre of water make a drink of a certain strength. Stir the same two spoonfuls into two litres instead and the drink tastes weaker, even though it holds exactly as much syrup. What changed is how much water the syrup is spread through.

In the last lesson the two compartments were the same size, so comparing amounts was enough. When the volumes differ, the strength of a solution is its concentration: the amount of solute divided by the volume it is dissolved in. The first drink has 2 spoonfuls in 1 litre, which is 2 spoonfuls per litre. The second has 2 spoonfuls in 2 litres, which is 1 spoonful per litre.

This gives a rule we will use all through the lesson. Adding water adds volume and no solute, so the concentration falls. Taking water away does the reverse and makes the solution stronger. The solute that was there stays there whatever happens to the water, and only the volume it fills changes.
One side of a membrane holds some solute in a known volume.
Now a jug in place of the cup.

Now put a membrane into the cup. Picture a container split in two by a membrane that lets water through and stops the solute. A membrane that passes some substances and blocks others like this is selectively permeable. Water crosses it in both directions, as it would cross any open gap.

Take two sides of equal size, one holding little solute and the other a lot. Solute particles take up room, so the side with more solute holds less water in each litre. By the rule from the last lesson, a substance drifts from where it is more crowded to where it is less crowded. For the water that means towards the side with more solute. The solute can't follow, because the membrane stops it, so the water goes to where the solute is. This net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane towards the side with more solute is called osmosis.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider and watch the dashed line between the two sides. The solute stays where it is, and the line slides as water crosses, until the two sides are equally concentrated. The side that gained water ends up larger. In these pictures nothing pushes on either side, so only the solute decides which way the water goes.

lead.text: The solute can't leave its own side, so only the water moves.
As the dashed line slides, the volumes change while the solute stays put, so the concentrations change too. To predict by how much, follow one side at a time.

Take a side with 6 units of solute in volume 2. Its concentration is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 units per volume. Now water enters until the volume is 3. The solute has not crossed, so it is still 6 units and the new concentration is 6 ÷ 3 = 2. More volume with the same solute makes a weaker solution.

Water leaving works in reverse. Take 12 units in volume 3, a concentration of 4. Water leaving takes none of the solute with it, so if water leaves until the volume is 2, the same 12 units are crowded into less space and the concentration becomes 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Volume and concentration move in opposite directions: doubling the volume halves the concentration, and halving the volume doubles it.
A real membrane has two sides, and both change at once. The side that gains water grows weaker and the side that loses it grows stronger, until the two concentrations match.
Keep the solute fixed and change the volume.
Back to the lettuce. The cells of the leaf have solute dissolved inside them, and the plain water in the bowl has none. By what we have just worked out, water moves into the cells.

In our pictures nothing pushes back, so water would keep entering for as long as the inside held more solute than the outside. A leaf cell is different. It sits inside the stiff cell wall we met in the first lesson, so when water enters the cell swells and presses against the wall. The wall presses back. The more water gets in, the harder the wall pushes.
The salty bowl has the opposite effect. The outside now holds more solute than the inside, so water leaves, the cells shrink away from their walls and lose their firmness, and the leaf goes limp.
Pressure is a second influence on how water moves, alongside the solute. Our diagrams leave it out, so a prediction about a real plant cell has to allow for it.
A plant cell sits in plain water, and water starts to enter it.

lessons.orientation: Predict osmosis without confusing solute amount with concentration.

blocks.text: Put a wilted lettuce leaf in a bowl of plain water for half an hour and it turns crisp again. Put a fresh leaf in a bowl of very salty water and it goes limp. Nobody has cut or heated either leaf, and the cells in both are wrapped in the same kind of membrane.

The last lesson ended with a membrane that passes water and stops a solute. A leaf cell's membrane behaves in just that way: most of what is dissolved in the cell and in the bowl is held back, while water can cross. That leaves water as the only thing free to move, so the answer must lie in where the water goes.
This lesson follows the water. To say where it goes, we first need a way of saying how strong a solution is, so we start with a cup of squash.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way water moves across a membrane when solute cannot, and work out how concentrations change.

recap.keyIdea: When only water can cross a membrane, it moves towards the side with more solute. The solute stays put, so volumes and concentrations change.

blocks.text: You diluted a drink, followed water towards the more concentrated side, and worked out new concentrations as the volume changed. That is enough to explain the lettuce. In plain water its cells take in water until the walls push back and the leaf turns crisp, and in salty water they lose water and the leaf goes limp.

lessons.title: Make a reaction easier

lead.text: A reaction rearranges molecules, and molecules do not rearrange just because they touch. Each reaction needs a push to get started. Think of a ball resting in a dip on one side of a hill, with a deeper valley beyond. Rolling into the valley would release energy, yet the ball stays where it is until something lifts it over the top. The height of that hill is the energy a reaction needs before it can begin, and it is called the activation energy.
In a warm beaker the molecules jostle and collide all the time. Only a few hit hard enough to climb the hill, so the reaction in beaker A runs slowly, at 4 units a minute.

afterFigure.text: Beaker B contains an enzyme, a protein that lowers the hill. With a lower hill, many more collisions are hard enough, so more molecules react every minute and beaker B makes 12 units a minute, three times as fast as A. The enzyme is not an ingredient and it is not used up. It comes out of each reaction unchanged and goes on to the next, so a small amount can speed up a very large number of reactions. What is left to explain is how a protein lowers the hill at all.

lead.text: The ball has to be lifted over the hill before it can roll into the valley.

An enzyme is a long chain folded into a particular three-dimensional shape, and on its surface there is a small dent, like the socket of a lock. The molecule an enzyme works on is called its substrate, and the dent that holds it is the active site. The substrate's shape matches the active site in the way a key matches a lock.

Once the substrate sits in the active site, the enzyme holds it in just the right position and the reaction needs far less of a push. When the product leaves, the active site is free for the next substrate molecule.

The fit also explains why enzymes are choosy. A dent shaped for one substrate will not hold a different molecule, so a cell needs a different enzyme for each reaction it wants to speed up. It also means that anything which changes the shape of the active site stops the enzyme working. The next screen looks at the most common cause.
A substrate sits in a dent that is shaped to match it.

steps.headline: What heat does to an enzyme

lead.text: Warm a beaker and its molecules move faster. They collide more often and harder, so more of them clear the hill, and an enzyme's reaction speeds up as the temperature rises.

A protein holds its shape through many weak attractions between different parts of the chain, and heat shakes those attractions loose. Above a certain temperature the chain starts to unfold, the active site loses its shape and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme is then denatured, which means its shape has changed so that it no longer works. The change is usually permanent. A raw egg white turns solid and white in a hot pan for the same reason: its proteins have lost their shape.

Warmth helps the collisions while heat damages the enzyme, so the two effects pull against each other. The rate climbs to a peak at its optimum, the temperature where the enzyme works best. After that it falls quickly. Because each enzyme has its own shape, each has its own optimum.
Enzyme A has been measured at four temperatures. The rate at the hottest one stays hidden until you have answered.

A set of enzyme results is usually a short list of rates, one for each temperature tried. To read it, find the largest rate and look along to its temperature. That temperature is the best of those tested, and the word tested matters: nothing in the list says what would have happened at a temperature nobody tried.

afterFigure.text: Enzyme B's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 1, 3, 7 and 11 units a minute. Its largest rate is 11, at 55°C. The rate was still climbing when the measurements stopped, so B's true optimum may be hotter than anything measured. Enzyme C peaks at 25°C and has already fallen by 40°C. Two enzymes can have quite different optimums, so 40°C cannot be named as the best temperature for every enzyme.

lead.text: Read the results for Enzyme A in the same way.
Each enzyme molecule has one active site, so it can hold one substrate molecule at a time. Think of a row of ticket counters, each serving one customer at a time at a steady pace.

Start with a few customers and plenty of free counters. Every customer is served at once, so each new arrival raises the number served per minute. Keep adding customers and sooner or later every counter is busy. After that, newcomers join a queue and the number served per minute stops rising.

afterFigure.text: An enzyme behaves the same way. With a fixed amount of enzyme the rate climbs as substrate is added and then levels off once every active site is busy, and more substrate cannot raise it any further. What lifts the ceiling is more enzyme, because that means more active sites. The second curve shows it.

lead.text: Think back to the ticket counters, with every counter busy and a queue forming.

Suppose someone adds an enzyme to a mixture and product appears quickly. That alone does not show the enzyme did it, because the mixture might have made product anyway, or the room might have been warmer that day. To judge the enzyme you need a comparison.

The comparison is a control: a second sample matched to the first in every way except that it has no enzyme. It has the same amounts, the same temperature and the same time. Only one thing differs, so any difference in the results can be put down to that one thing. Repeating the test on several samples helps too, because it shows whether a difference is a one-off.

To measure the effect, subtract the control from the enzyme sample at the same moment. If the enzyme sample has made 20 units after two minutes and the control has made 8, the enzyme accounts for the extra 12. Rates add up over time in the same way. A sample making 8 units a minute and a control making 5 differ by 3 units a minute, so after four minutes the gap is 12 units.
A sample with the enzyme and a matched control were measured over three minutes.

blocks.text: Two beakers stand side by side on a bench, holding the same mixture at the same temperature, and the same reaction is running in both. Beaker A makes 4 units of product every minute. Beaker B has one extra ingredient, a helper molecule. With its help the reaction makes 12 units every minute.
When the run is over the helper is still in beaker B, in the same amount as before. It took part in every one of the reactions and came out of each one unchanged.

A cell needs this kind of help. It runs thousands of reactions at once, and left alone most of them would be far too slow to keep it alive. This lesson asks what a helper molecule does to a reaction and what heat does to the helper. It then asks what limits how fast the helper can work, and how a scientist can show that a speed-up really came from it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how a helper molecule speeds up a reaction, read data about it and judge a test of it.

recap.keyIdea: An enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy. Its effect depends on its shape and its amount, and a matched control shows what it did.

blocks.text: Beaker B ran three times as fast as beaker A because its enzyme lowered the activation energy. An enzyme works because its shape fits its substrate, and heat can spoil that fit. A fixed amount of enzyme caps the rate, and a matched control lets you credit a difference to the enzyme.

recap.nextHook: Plants use enzymes to build the sugar that makes up their bodies, and the next lesson starts with a sapling that gains 75 kg while the soil it grows in loses only 60 grams.

lessons.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lead.text: Start with what the tree is made of. Wood, leaves and roots are built mostly from carbon-based molecules such as sugars and the long chains made from them, and those molecules also contain hydrogen and oxygen. So the tree's extra 75 kg is mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms that were not in the tree before.

The soil cannot be their main source, because it lost only 60 grams while the tree gained 75 kilograms, over a thousand times as much. The rainwater supplies hydrogen and oxygen. Carbon is the harder one, because water holds almost none. The only large store of carbon within reach of a leaf is the air, where it travels as carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out. A leaf takes carbon dioxide in through tiny pores and builds its carbon into sugar.
Light does not supply atoms. Sunshine is energy, and energy is not made of matter. It plays a different part, which comes a few screens later.
Rainwater carries almost no carbon, and light carries none at all.

steps.headline: Building sugar from air and water

lead.text: A leaf does this job in its cells, in the chloroplasts you met in the first lesson. The process is called photosynthesis, which means putting together with light. The leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from its roots, and uses light energy to join them into a sugar called glucose. Oxygen is left over, and the leaf releases it to the air.

Chemists write this as an equation. Each formula stands for one molecule, and the number in front says how many molecules take part: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Read it as six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules, with light, making one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules. The small numbers inside a formula count atoms, so C₆H₁₂O₆ is a molecule built from 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms.

afterFigure.text: Glucose is the sugar the leaf makes first, and the rest of its chemistry starts from it. The figure shows the equation for one glucose and for two, and the next screens count atoms through it.

lead.text: The number written in front of a formula counts molecules.

The equation also lets you follow the atoms. Atoms are rearranged in a reaction and are never created or destroyed, so every carbon atom in the glucose must have come from a carbon atom that went in. The only carbon on the left of the equation is in carbon dioxide, and each CO₂ molecule holds exactly one carbon atom.
A glucose molecule holds six carbon atoms, so it takes six CO₂ molecules to supply them. Make five glucose molecules and the leaf needs 5 × 6 = 30 carbon atoms, so it takes in 30 CO₂ molecules.

The other numbers in the equation scale the same way. Every glucose is made with six water molecules and comes with six oxygen molecules, so five glucose molecules use 30 water molecules and release 30 oxygen molecules. Scaling up from one glucose is multiplication.
Use the same counting for a smaller batch.

Atoms are only half of the story. Joining carbon dioxide and water into glucose takes work, because the glucose holds more energy than the molecules that went into it. That energy comes from light. The chloroplasts catch some of the light that falls on the leaf and use it to build the glucose.
The energy is not lost when it is used. It is stored in the bonds that hold the glucose together, and energy stored in this way is called chemical energy.

So the atoms and the energy reach the leaf by different routes. The atoms come from carbon dioxide and water, and the energy comes from light and ends up as chemical energy in the glucose. The sugar is a store that the leaf can draw on later, even in the dark. How a cell gets the energy back out is the subject of the next lesson.
The glucose is more than a heap of atoms.

A leaf makes sugar faster in brighter light, up to a point. Measure the rate at different light levels and plot it, and the curve rises at first and then flattens, so that brighter light makes no more difference.

afterFigure.text: A flat curve means that something else is holding the rate down. Photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and water together, and it can go no faster than the scarcest of them allows. Whatever is in shortest supply is the limiting factor. In the figure the leaf with less carbon dioxide levels off sooner and lower, and the leaf with more carbon dioxide keeps climbing. For the lower curve the limit is the carbon dioxide supply and not the light. Extra light helps only while light is the thing in short supply.

lead.text: A leaf was given a fixed, low supply of CO₂. Its rate was measured at several light levels. Compare two readings to see what extra light did.

lessons.orientation: Trace carbon and energy through the overall photosynthesis reaction.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Suppose you plant a sapling in a large tub of soil. The sapling weighs 2 kg. You dry and weigh the soil as well, and then you give the tree nothing but rainwater for years.
When it has grown the tree weighs 77 kg, which is 75 kg more than it started with. You weigh the soil again. It has lost only 60 grams.

Matter cannot appear from nothing, so the 75 kg must have come from somewhere other than the soil. This lesson follows the atoms in the tree's body back to where they came from, using the numbers and what a tree is made of as clues. It then writes down the process that built them and looks at the energy that drives it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say where a leaf's carbon comes from, count molecules with the overall equation and keep matter and energy apart.

recap.keyIdea: Photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies the energy, which the plant stores in the sugar.

blocks.text: The tree's extra 75 kg came from the air and from water, and almost none of it from the soil. You counted how many molecules of carbon dioxide, water and oxygen go with each glucose, and you kept the atoms, which come from the gases and water, apart from the energy, which comes from light. A flat curve showed that something other than light was setting the pace.

recap.nextHook: The glucose a leaf makes stores energy, and the next lesson starts with a burning candle to see how a cell gets that energy back out.

lessons.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

lead.text: Cells run on the same sort of reaction as the candle, but they carry it out in a long chain of small steps, each one helped by an enzyme. Because each step releases only a little energy, the cell never overheats, and it can capture part of the energy at every stage. The set of reactions that transfers energy from a fuel such as glucose is called respiration. When it uses oxygen it is called aerobic respiration.

Written as an equation, aerobic respiration of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, with energy transferred. Put it beside the equation from the last lesson and it runs the other way. A leaf builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and a cell takes glucose apart again. Animal cells get their glucose from food. Plant cells make theirs, and light supplies the energy at the start of the loop.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the two equations side by side. The atoms go round the loop, and the energy comes in as light and goes out as work and heat.

lead.text: The candle's wax left as carbon dioxide and water vapour. A cell's sugar leaves in much the same way.

A cell cannot spend glucose directly on its work. Instead, much of the energy released from glucose is used to build a small molecule called ATP, which works like a rechargeable battery. The mitochondria you met in the first lesson do most of this job. The cell then spends ATP wherever work is needed, such as moving parts of the cell, building new molecules and pushing substances across a membrane.
None of this is perfectly efficient. A good share of the energy cannot be captured in ATP and is given out as heat. That is why a crowded room warms up and why your body stays warm without a flame.
A cell uses up and rebuilds its ATP all the time. It is better to think of ATP as the way a cell carries energy to the place where it is needed than as a store of fuel.
A cell needs a way to carry energy from where sugar is taken apart to where work is done.

Next come the atoms. As in photosynthesis, atoms are rearranged in respiration and none are created or destroyed. The carbon atoms in glucose have to end up somewhere, and the equation shows where: all of them leave in carbon dioxide. Nothing is turned into energy. Energy is a separate matter, carried by ATP and given off as heat.

Every carbon atom ends up in exactly one CO₂ molecule, and a glucose holds six carbon atoms, so the count is simple. Three glucose molecules hold 3 × 6 = 18 carbon atoms, and breaking them down completely produces 18 CO₂ molecules. Count the carbon atoms in the fuel and you know how many CO₂ molecules are made.
Use the same counting for two glucose molecules.

People often use breathing and respiration as if they meant the same thing, and the difference matters. Breathing is the movement of air in and out of your lungs. It brings oxygen close to your blood and carries carbon dioxide away. Respiration is the chemistry inside your cells that uses that oxygen and the sugar. The two are linked, because breathing supplies what respiration needs, but one is a movement of air and the other a set of reactions.

A plant shows the difference clearly. It has no lungs and does not breathe, yet every one of its living cells respires. It makes glucose in the light and respires all the time, in the dark as well, because cells need ATP at every hour of the day. Light is needed to build the sugar and not to release its energy. Bacteria and mushrooms have no lungs either, and they respire too.
Both words come up whenever people talk about oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Respiration is hard to watch, but its effects can be measured. A living thing sealed in a jar uses up the oxygen as it respires, so the oxygen in the jar falls. Measure the amount at the start and again after a few minutes, and the difference is the oxygen the living thing used.

afterFigure.text: Careful experimenters also set up a blank, an identical jar with no living things in it. The blank shows what the apparatus does by itself, such as a little oxygen dissolving into water or a slight leak. In the figure the jar with organisms loses 6 units of oxygen in three minutes and the blank loses 1, so the organisms themselves used 6 − 1 = 5. Without the blank, the whole fall of 6 would be put down to the organisms.

lead.text: A sealed jar of living organisms loses oxygen as they respire.
Now the blank jar joins in. It is identical to the organism jar but holds no living things.

lessons.orientation: Connect respiration, ATP and conserved atoms without confusing breathing with cellular reactions.
lessons.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A candle burns wax with oxygen from the air. The flame gives out heat and light, and the wax leaves as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Hold a cold glass over the flame and the water condenses on it as mist.

A cell does something very like this with sugar. It combines the sugar with oxygen, and the sugar leaves as carbon dioxide and water, just as the wax did. The energy stored in the sugar is released too. Yet a cell cannot flare up like a flame, because it would cook itself if all that energy came out as heat at once.

So the cell has to release the energy in small steps and catch it in a form it can spend. This lesson follows a molecule of sugar into a cell and finds where its atoms and its energy end up. At the close, a sealed jar shows how to measure the process.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how a cell gets energy from sugar, follow its carbon atoms and tell breathing from what happens inside cells.

recap.keyIdea: Respiration transfers energy from fuel into ATP, and conserves the fuel's atoms in its products. Breathing is not the same thing.

blocks.text: A cell takes sugar apart in small steps, the way a candle burns wax in one go. The energy is caught in ATP or given off as heat, and every carbon atom of the sugar leaves in a molecule of carbon dioxide. Breathing only brings the oxygen in. You counted the CO₂ that a few glucose molecules produce, and you measured oxygen use in a sealed jar after taking off what the blank jar lost.

recap.nextHook: Respiration keeps a cell's work going, and the next lesson turns to a job a cell must do before it divides: copying a long message exactly, using two strips that zip together.

lessons.title: Copy a message one base at a time

steps.headline: The letters of a DNA strand

lead.text: A DNA strand is a long chain with a row of small units called bases along it. There are four kinds, named adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine, and written A, T, C and G. The order of the bases along a strand is the message, in the way the order of letters makes a sentence.

A DNA molecule has two strands lying side by side, and each base on one strand is joined to a base on the other. A base joins with one kind of partner only. A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. A joined pair is called a base pair. Like the teeth of a zip, the two strands fit together in only one way.
One base decides which base can sit opposite it.

Because A always faces T and C always faces G, each strand is an exact match for the other. Each is the complement of the other, and the two strands are described as complementary. To find the complement, go along a strand and swap every base for its partner. For the strand GATC, G becomes C, A becomes T, T becomes A and C becomes G, so the partner reads CTAG.

afterFigure.text: When a cell copies DNA it uses this rule. A strand that is used to build its partner is called a template, because the new strand takes its form from it. The two strands of real DNA run in opposite directions, which is why their ends are labelled 5′ and 3′. To keep things simple we write each partner directly beneath its strand, base for base.

lead.text: Swap each base for its partner, working along the strand in order.

Now the zip from the start of the lesson can be made exact. Before a cell divides, enzymes unzip a DNA molecule along its length and pull the two strands apart. The bases that were joined are left exposed, and each strand becomes a template.

Free bases in the cell line up against the exposed bases by the pairing rule, and an enzyme joins them into a new strand. This copying is called replication. Each old strand ends up with a brand-new partner that fits it exactly. Every new base is placed by the template, so the new strand is the exact complement of the old one and has exactly as many bases.

The result is two DNA molecules where there was one. Each is made of one old strand and one new strand. Because each molecule keeps half of the original, the method is called semiconservative replication.
After the strands have each been given a partner, count what is zipped together.

A cell's DNA is divided into separate long molecules. Each one, packed with proteins, forms a structure called a chromosome. A human body cell has 46 of them, and counting chromosomes means counting these structures.

When a chromosome is replicated, its two identical DNA molecules stay joined side by side. Each copy is called a sister chromatid, and the joined pair is still counted as one chromosome. So a cell with two chromosomes has two chromosomes after copying as well, but each now holds two DNA molecules, four in all.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a cell before and after copying. The amount of DNA doubles, from two molecules to four, while the number of chromosomes stays at two. Chromosomes are counted as the joined structures and DNA molecules are counted as chromatids, and the two numbers agree only before copying.

lead.text: The two copies stay attached to each other after replication.
Copying has just happened in a cell. The amount of DNA has changed, so look carefully at what the question counts.

lessons.orientation: Use complementary DNA bases and distinguish DNA amount from chromosome count.
lessons.reviewLabel: Copy a message one base at a time
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of a zip, which has two strips lined with teeth, where the teeth on one strip fit the gaps between the teeth on the other. Pull it open and you have two loose strips. Suppose each loose strip is now given a brand-new partner that is built from scratch to fit it exactly. The pairs are then zipped up again.

You started with one zipped pair and finished with two. Each new pair holds one strip from the original and one strip that did not exist a moment ago. A cell does something very like this before it divides. Its instructions are written in DNA, a molecule so long that the DNA in one human cell would stretch about two metres if it were pulled straight, and the cell has to make an exact second copy for the new cell.

The zip is a good picture because it shows the trick: the shape of one strip decides the shape of its partner. This lesson looks at what the strips are made of and how one strand fixes the other. It ends with what copying does to the way a cell's DNA is counted.

intro.promise: By the end you'll copy a DNA strand base by base and say what each new molecule keeps.

recap.keyIdea: Each strand of DNA is a template, so each new molecule keeps one old strand. Copying doubles the DNA but not the chromosome count.

blocks.text: Each strand of DNA fixed the order of its partner, so copying turned one molecule into two, each with one old strand and one new. You worked out the partners of two strands base by base. You also saw that copying doubles the DNA and leaves the chromosome count alone: a cell with 4 chromosomes still has 4 afterwards, now made of 8 chromatids.

recap.nextHook: Copied chromosomes are ready to be shared out, and the next lesson begins with a teacher who photocopies a five-page worksheet and hands the original to one student and the copy to another.

lessons.title: Make two cells

lead.text: In the last lesson each chromosome was copied and ended up as two sister chromatids joined side by side. The worksheet picture helps here: the joined pair is like a page with its photocopy stapled to it. Mitosis is the stage in which the cell shares these copies out. The chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell, and the two sister chromatids of each one are pulled apart towards opposite ends.

Once the chromatids separate, each counts as a chromosome of its own. Each end of the cell now holds one complete set, and a new nucleus forms around each set. The cell then pinches into two in a step called cytokinesis. The two cells that result are called daughter cells.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a cell with six chromosomes, once its DNA is copied and again after it has divided. Compare the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell with the number in the parent. The copying came first, and the sharing keeps the number the same.

lead.text: Think of the worksheet. Each student received a complete set. A daughter cell needs a complete set of chromosomes too.

Counting gets tricky between copying and dividing, because chromosomes and DNA molecules are no longer the same number. Before copying, each chromosome is one DNA molecule. After copying, each chromosome has two sister chromatids, and each chromatid is one complete copy of the chromosome's DNA, so each chromosome holds two DNA molecules.

afterFigure.text: To count DNA molecules after copying, count two for every chromosome. A cell with 3 chromosomes has 3 × 2 = 6 DNA molecules. The count also runs backwards. A cell showing 8 DNA molecules after copying must have had 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes, which is the cell in the figure. In both directions the number of chromosomes stays the same, because copying changes only the number of DNA molecules.

lead.text: Each of the six chromosomes has been copied.

Each round of mitosis turns every dividing cell into two, so a group of dividing cells doubles in number each time. One cell becomes 2 cells in the first round. Both of those divide in the second round, giving 4 cells. After any number of rounds the count is 2 multiplied by itself once for each round.

afterFigure.text: This is the ideal case, in which every cell divides in every round. It describes the first days of an embryo well, when a fertilised egg divides again and again, but it cannot last. In your body most cells divide only when they are needed, and the next screen looks at that.

lead.text: In the ideal case every cell divides once in each round.

Cells divide for growth and repair, and in some organisms for reproduction. A cut on your hand heals because the cells at its edges divide to fill the gap. Once the gap is closed the division stops. Signals from neighbouring cells and conditions in the tissue switch division on and off, so division is regulated. A tissue makes the cells it needs and then stops.

Regulation changes the arithmetic. In a real tissue only some of the cells divide in a given round. Take a tissue of 6 cells in which a third of them divide. The 2 cells that divide become 4, and the other 4 do not divide, so the tissue now holds 4 + 4 = 8 cells. It has grown by 2, which is far less than the doubling to 12 that you would get if every cell divided.
In a different tissue, only half of the cells divide in one round.

lessons.orientation: Track chromosomes through mitotic division and connect division to growth and repair.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A teacher has a worksheet of 5 pages and wants two students to work on it. She photocopies the whole set once, hands the original set to one student and gives the copy to the other.

Each student now holds a complete set. The teacher did not tear the worksheet in half and give each student a few pages, because neither student could then do the work. She copied first and shared afterwards, so every page exists twice and each student gets one of each.

A cell that divides faces the same job with its chromosomes. Both new cells must carry the full set of instructions, so the DNA has to be copied first and then shared out, with each new cell receiving one copy of every chromosome. The last lesson ended with the copying. This lesson looks at the sharing and counts what it produces. It then watches many rounds of division build up a tissue.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosomes through mitosis and count cells as a tissue grows.

recap.keyIdea: Mitosis copies the DNA and then shares it, so each daughter cell keeps the parent's chromosome number. Regulation decides which cells divide.

blocks.text: Mitosis copies the DNA and then shares it out, so a daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as its parent. You followed 4 chromosomes into each daughter cell and counted the DNA molecules in a copied cell. You also counted cells through three ideal doublings and through a tissue where only half of the cells divide.

recap.nextHook: Mitosis gives every daughter cell the same number of chromosomes as its parent, and the next lesson begins with a puzzle that this rule cannot solve: an egg and a sperm each come from a body cell with 46 chromosomes, yet they join to make a first cell that must also have 46.

lessons.title: Halve a chromosome set

lead.text: Your 46 chromosomes are not 46 different things. They are 23 pairs. In each pair one chromosome came from your mother and the other from your father, and the two match: they carry the same genes, in the same order along their length. Think of two copies of a recipe book, each written out by a different person. Every chapter appears in both books, but the wording of a recipe may differ a little between them.

The two chromosomes of a matching pair are called homologous chromosomes. A cell that holds two of every chromosome, one set from each parent, is called diploid. Your body cells are diploid, which is why 23 pairs make 23 × 2 = 46 chromosomes.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows cells with two pairs and with three pairs. Real cells have more pairs, but the counting works the same way: the number of pairs, times 2, gives the number of chromosomes.

lead.text: Use the idea of a matching pair. Count chromosomes, not pairs.

The puzzle from the opening has a plain answer: an egg or a sperm does not carry 46 chromosomes. Eggs and sperm are called gametes, and a gamete holds a single set, with one chromosome from each pair. A cell with a single set is called haploid. In a human, that means a gamete carries one of each of the 23 kinds of chromosome.

Fertilisation is the joining of an egg and a sperm. The two haploid sets come together in the first cell of a new person, which is diploid again, with one set from each parent. That is why you carry one chromosome of each pair from your mother and the other from your father.

afterFigure.text: So the body needs a step that turns a diploid cell into haploid ones, and each of them must receive a full single set, with one chromosome from every pair and none missing. The figure compares a cell with three pairs and the cells that should come from it. Mitosis cannot do this job, because it gives each daughter cell the parent's full diploid set. A different kind of division is needed.

lead.text: Think of a baby's first cell and the two gametes that made it.

The special division is called meiosis. It begins as mitosis does: the cell copies its DNA once, so every chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined together, like the stapled page and photocopy from the last lesson. Then the cell divides twice in a row, with no more copying in between.

The first division, meiosis I, is where the number falls. The two chromosomes of each homologous pair line up side by side, and the division pulls them apart, one to each end of the cell. The sister chromatids stay joined and travel together. Each new cell receives one chromosome from every pair, which is one full set.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the cell has three pairs. After the first division there are two cells, each with 3 chromosomes, down from 6. Each of those chromosomes is still a joined pair of chromatids, so each cell holds 6 DNA molecules for now. The chromosome number has halved, but the cells are not finished.

lead.text: Meiosis I separates one kind of chromosome partner, and that separation is what halves the number.

Each cell now has half the chromosomes, but every chromosome is still two joined sister chromatids. The second division, meiosis II, deals with those. It works as mitosis does: the chromosomes line up, and the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite ends of each cell.

No copying happens between the two divisions. The single round of copying at the start serves both, so the DNA is shared out twice after being copied once. When meiosis II is done, each of the two cells has split in two. The result is four cells.

afterFigure.text: Count the cells in the figure. Each of the four has 3 chromosomes, and each chromosome is now a single chromatid, so each cell holds 3 DNA molecules. A parent cell with 3 × 2 = 6 chromosomes ends as four haploid cells with 3 each. The number halved once, in meiosis I, and stayed at 3 in meiosis II, because that division only separates sister chromatids.

lead.text: A starting cell has two homologous pairs. Follow the chromosomes through both divisions.

steps.headline: Why no two gametes are alike

lead.text: Meiosis does more than halve the count. Look again at meiosis I. In each pair, one chromosome came from your mother and the other from your father, and which one goes to which end of the cell is a matter of chance. With three pairs, each pair can split in two ways, so a cell can produce 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 different combinations.

Humans have 23 pairs, so the shuffle alone can give 2 multiplied by itself 23 times, which is over 8 million different combinations. On top of that, the two chromosomes of a pair swap matching segments with each other before the first division. This swapping is called crossing over, and it means a single chromosome in a gamete can be a patchwork of your mother's and your father's versions.

Fertilisation adds a final layer of chance, because any egg may meet any sperm. Brothers and sisters share the same parents and the same number of chromosomes, yet each one is a different draw from an enormous number of possibilities.
Two siblings have the same parents and the same number of chromosomes, yet they are not identical.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish homologues from sister chromatids and follow two meiotic divisions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Nearly every cell in your body holds 46 chromosomes, and the last lesson showed how mitosis passes all 46 to each new cell. You began as a single cell, though, made when an egg and a sperm joined. That first cell also held 46 chromosomes, and every cell in you descends from it.

Suppose the egg and the sperm had each come from an ordinary body cell and kept all 46. On joining they would make a first cell with 46 + 46 = 92. Mitosis would pass 92 to every cell of the baby, and the baby's own egg or sperm would carry 92 into the next generation. That generation's first cell would hold 184, and each generation after it would double the number again.

Something has to cut the number down before an egg or a sperm is made, and it has to leave each one with a usable set. This lesson follows the chromosomes through that step and counts them at every stage. It also shows why the same step explains how you can resemble your parents without being a copy of either.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow chromosome numbers through the two divisions of meiosis and through fertilisation.

recap.keyIdea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so gametes are haploid. Fertilisation restores diploid cells with a new mix of chromosomes.

blocks.text: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, so one diploid cell makes four haploid gametes. You counted a cell with three pairs down from 6 chromosomes to 3 in each of four cells, and worked out that an egg carries 23 of a baby's 46.
You also saw why the shuffle of chromosomes and the swapping of segments make every gamete different.

recap.nextHook: Meiosis hands each gamete one chromosome from every pair, and which one it gets is a matter of chance. The next lesson treats that chance like a coin toss and asks what the children of two parents could inherit.

lessons.title: What could the offspring inherit?

lead.text: Genes come in versions. A pea plant's flower colour gene has one version that gives purple flowers and another that gives white. The different versions of a gene are called alleles, and geneticists label them with letters: a capital such as A for one allele and the small a for the other.

A diploid plant has two chromosomes in each homologous pair, so it carries two alleles of each gene, one on each chromosome. The pair of alleles it carries is its genotype. A plant with the genotype AA has two copies of the same allele. A plant with the genotype Aa has two different alleles, and a genotype like that is called heterozygous.

When a gamete is made, meiosis I pulls the two chromosomes of a pair apart, so each gamete carries just one of the two alleles. Which one it gets is a matter of chance. An Aa plant makes gametes that carry A about half the time and a about half the time, like a coin that lands heads or tails.
Look at the two alleles of the Aa plant and ask whether they match.

Go back to the two coins. Write the first coin's results, H and T, across the top of a table. Write the second coin's results down the side. Each of the four boxes is one outcome, such as HH or TH. The table makes sure no outcome is missed, and every box is equally likely.

A Punnett square is the same table for a cross between two parents. Write one parent's gametes along the top and the other parent's down the side, and fill each box with the two alleles that meet. For two Aa parents each gamete carries A or a, so the boxes read AA, Aa, aA and aa. The order of the letters makes no difference, so aA is just another Aa.

afterFigure.text: That gives one box AA, two boxes Aa and one box aa, out of four. The chance of a genotype is the number of its boxes divided by the total number of boxes. Aa fills two boxes because the A can come from either parent: the pollen can bring A and the egg a, or the other way round.

lead.text: Use the boxes of the square for two Aa parents.

The genotype is hidden inside the plant. What you can see is its phenotype, the trait it shows, such as purple or white flowers. Two different genotypes can give the same phenotype. In pea plants the A allele is dominant: one copy of it is enough to give purple flowers, so both AA and Aa plants are purple. The a allele is recessive. It shows only when no A is present, so only aa plants are white.

Take a cross of AA with Aa. Every box of the square holds at least one A, so every offspring is purple, even though half of them are Aa and carry a hidden a. Two plants can look identical and still have different genotypes.

afterFigure.text: Reading the square also works in reverse. If two purple plants have a white offspring, that offspring is aa and must have received an a from each parent. Each purple parent must carry an a, which means both of them are Aa.

lead.text: A heterozygous plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant. Fill the four boxes, then decide which of them show the recessive trait.

A Punnett square gives a chance for each offspring, and every offspring is a fresh draw. Think of a coin that has just landed heads three times. The next toss is still an even toss, because the coin has no memory of the earlier ones. Two Aa plants behave in the same way: every seed has a 25% chance of being aa, whatever happened to the seeds before it.

So the square makes no promise that exactly one seed in four will be white. Four coin tosses can easily give three heads, and four seeds from an Aa × Aa cross can easily give two white plants or none. The percentages describe what to expect on average across a great many seeds. In a small family, chance can pull the results well away from them.
Four seeds come from a cross of two Aa plants, and the square gives the chance of aa for each one.

lessons.orientation: Use a single-gene cross while separating genotype, phenotype and probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Flip a fair coin and it lands heads or tails, each equally likely. Flip two coins, one after the other, and the pair of results can be heads then heads, heads then tails, tails then heads or tails then tails. That makes four outcomes. Each coin is fair, so all four are equally likely, and the chance of two heads is one outcome out of four.

The last lesson ended with meiosis handing each gamete one chromosome from every pair, chosen by chance. That is a coin toss of a kind. Suppose a pea plant carries two different versions of a gene for flower colour, one on each chromosome of a pair. Each of its pollen grains and egg cells gets one version or the other, with equal chance. A second plant does the same, and a seed gets one version from each.

That sets the problem for this lesson. Given two parent plants, find the chance that a seed grows into a plant with purple flowers and the chance that it grows into one with white flowers. Counting outcomes, as with the coins, gives the answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a Punnett square to work out the chance of each genotype and trait in a cross of two parents.

recap.keyIdea: Each parent passes on one allele at random, and a Punnett square counts the equally likely pairings. The chances apply to each child.

blocks.text: You listed the equally likely outcomes for two coins and for two Aa parents, and read 25% aa and 50% recessive from the squares. You also saw that a family of four need not follow the percentages.

recap.nextHook: Every cross in this lesson began with alleles that already existed. Somewhere an allele has to appear for the first time, and the next lesson starts with a scribe who copies a page by hand and now and then slips.

lessons.title: Where does a new variant come from?

lead.text: Copying slips have a name. A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA. A cell's slips come in the same kinds as the scribe's. One base can be swapped for another, which is called a substitution. A base can be added, which is an insertion, and a base can be left out, which is a deletion.

A substitution replaces one base with another, so the length of the DNA stays the same: a gene of 600 bases is still 600 bases long afterwards. Insertions and deletions change the length. Cells copy with great care and repair most slips, but copying errors and damage to DNA both happen, and neither happens for a reason. A mutation arises by chance, in the way a typing slip does.

The scribe's rate gives the idea of scale. At one slip in every 100 words, a page of 500 words carries on average 500 ÷ 100 = 5 slips. Biologists make the same kind of calculation for DNA: how many changes should turn up in this many bases at this rate.
Look at which base changed and what stayed the same.

To find a mutation you compare the copy with the original. Write the two sequences one above the other so that they line up, and compare them position by position from the left. Wherever the two bases match, nothing has changed. Wherever they differ, that base has changed.

Take ACGT and AGGT. The first pair is A and A, which matches. The second pair is C and G, which differs. The last two pairs match again. Exactly one position differs, so one base has changed: a C became a G, which is a substitution.

afterFigure.text: Finding a changed base shows only that the DNA has changed. It says nothing about what the change does. Some changes damage a protein badly, some alter it slightly and some have no noticeable effect, and telling which needs evidence about the organism as well as the sequence.

lead.text: Compare the two sequences position by position, and count only the pairs that disagree.

Not every mutation can be passed on. A mutation lives in the cell where it happens and in the cells that descend from that cell by mitosis. A mutation in a skin cell is copied into the skin cells that grow from it and stays in that one body. When the person has children, it does not go with them.

A child inherits only what is in the gametes that made it. A mutation in the line of cells that make eggs or sperm can end up in a gamete. If that gamete takes part in fertilisation, every cell of the child carries the change, because every cell descends from that first cell. The parents need not carry the change anywhere else in their bodies. This is how a new allele can enter a family, and eventually a species.
Think about which cells take part in fertilisation.

steps.headline: Chance makes variants, selection sorts them

lead.text: A mutation does not arise because the organism would benefit from it. Mutations happen by chance, whether the change helps, harms or makes no difference. Most make little or no difference. A few harm, and a very few help in the environment where the organism lives.

What happens next is a separate matter. Suppose a few bacteria in a large group carry a variant that lets them survive an antibiotic. The variant was there before the drug arrived, the result of an earlier chance mutation. When the drug kills the other bacteria, the survivors multiply, and a much larger share of the group now carries the variant. This sorting is called selection: a variant that helps its carriers leave more offspring becomes more common.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows one variant drawn blue and another drawn gold, before and after a sorting like this. Selection changed how common each variant is. The helpful variant was already present, so the environment only decided which ones were left.

lead.text: Think about whether the organism or the environment decides which new variants appear.
After an environmental change, one variant becomes more common in a group of organisms.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish DNA change from directed need and identify what can be inherited.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a new variant come from?

blocks.text: A scribe is copying a page of 500 words by hand. She is careful and she checks her work, but on average she slips once in every 100 words. A slip might swap a letter for another, miss a letter out or write one twice. The copy she hands over is almost the same as the original, and where it differs, nobody told her to change it.

Now think about the instructions inside a cell. Every time a cell divides it copies its DNA, which is a very long page written in four letters, and a human cell holds about six billion of them. Cells check their copies and repair most slips, but over billions of letters a few are bound to get through.

The last lesson used alleles such as A and a as if they had always existed. Each one had to appear for the first time somewhere, and a slip in copying is one way that happens. This lesson looks at those slips: what they look like, how to spot one by comparing a copy with its original, which ones can reach a child and what decides whether a new version spreads.

intro.promise: By the end you'll spot a mutation by comparing sequences and say which mutations can be inherited and why they are not made to order.

recap.keyIdea: A mutation is a chance change in DNA sequence, and only one in a gamete's line of cells can be inherited. Selection sorts variants and does not order them.

blocks.text: You compared sequences position by position and counted the bases that differed, and you saw that a substitution leaves a gene's length alone. You also traced which mutations reach children and saw that selection sorts variants without ordering them.

recap.nextHook: Mutations supply the variants and selection decides which become common. The next lesson starts in a meadow of beetles, where birds find some colours easier to spot than others.

lessons.title: A population changes over generations

lead.text: Start by counting. At the beginning there are 16 blue beetles and 24 gold ones, 40 in all. A group of one kind of living thing in one place is a population, and the different forms within it, such as blue and gold, are variants. To say how common a variant is, we use its frequency, which is its count divided by the size of the whole population, usually written as a percentage.

Here the blue beetles have a frequency of 16 ÷ 40 = 0.4, which is 40%, and the gold beetles have 24 ÷ 40 = 60%. Frequency is useful because it ignores the size of the group. A meadow with twice as many beetles, 32 blue and 48 gold, has the same frequencies, since 32 ÷ 80 = 40%. A count says how many beetles there are. A frequency says what share of the population they make.
Divide the count of the variant by the size of the whole group.

steps.headline: What the birds did to the shares

lead.text: Back to the meadow. The birds eat half of the 16 blue beetles, which leaves 8. The 24 gold beetles are untouched. The meadow now holds 8 + 24 = 32 beetles. The blue frequency has changed to 8 ÷ 32 = 25%, down from 40% before.

The size of a change in frequency is the difference between the two percentages. A frequency is already a percentage, so we call that difference percentage points: 40% − 25% = 15 percentage points. The blue frequency fell by 15 points. Saying points avoids a muddle between a fall of 15 points and a fall of 15 percent of 40, which would be only 6 points.

afterFigure.text: The survivors are the parents of the next generation. Suppose each beetle leaves two offspring and colour passes from parent to young. Then 8 blue beetles leave 16 blue young and 24 gold beetles leave 48 gold young. The new generation has 64 beetles, and the blue frequency is 16 ÷ 64 = 25%. What the birds changed in one season has been carried into the next generation.

lead.text: Work out each frequency first, then find the difference between them.

What happened in the meadow has a name. In any population the individuals differ. Some differences are heritable, which means they pass from parents to offspring. The beetles' colour is one, since blue parents tend to have blue young. Other differences, such as a scratch on a wing, are not heritable, because the young are born without them.

Natural selection happens when the carriers of one heritable variant leave more offspring than the carriers of another, in the environment where they live. The variant that does better then makes up a bigger share of each new generation, and its frequency rises generation after generation. Here the birds favoured the gold beetles, which were more likely to survive and breed.
Nobody decides this. No beetle changes colour to hide, and no bird intends to alter the meadow. The shift happens because some variants leave more offspring than others.
Think about what is changing the shares of the variants in the meadow.

Whether a variant helps depends on where it lives. Blue is a handicap on dry golden grass, because the birds spot it. Move the beetles to a woodland floor carpeted in bluebells, and it is the gold beetles that stand out. The same variants face the same birds and the result is the opposite one.

In the figure the same mixed group of 40 beetles, 20 blue and 20 gold, is placed in two environments. In environment A, the bluebell wood, the blue beetles do well and their frequency rises from 50% to 70%. In environment B, the golden meadow, the blue beetles do badly and their frequency falls to 30%. The beetles are the same in both places. Only the environment differs.

afterFigure.text: So a trait is neither good nor bad by itself. A variant that rises in one environment can fall in another, and when an environment changes, the same variant can go from an advantage to a handicap.

lead.text: In a golden meadow the blue beetles do badly, as in environment B.

A change in frequency shows that something happened. It does not show that selection did it. Chance alone can change the shares, especially in a small population. Take 10 beetles, 5 blue and 5 gold, and suppose a storm kills 6 of them without regard to colour. By bad luck 4 of the 6 are gold and 2 are blue. The 4 survivors are 3 blue and 1 gold, so the blue frequency has risen from 5 ÷ 10 = 50% to 3 ÷ 4 = 75%. That is a rise of 25 points with no advantage behind it.

Migration can do the same thing. If 40 gold beetles fly in to a meadow of 20 blue and 20 gold, the blue frequency falls from 50% to 20 ÷ 80 = 25%, whatever the birds do. To credit natural selection you need evidence that the variants really differ in the offspring they leave, and a shift in the shares cannot supply that on its own.
A variant has become more common in a small population.

lessons.orientation: Connect heritable variation and reproductive success without confusing change with proof of cause.
