blocks.text: A meadow of dry golden grass is home to 40 beetles. Sixteen are bright blue and 24 are gold. The gold ones are hard to see against the grass, while the blue ones show up from the air, and a flock of birds that hunt by sight has found the meadow.

Before the beetles have a chance to breed, the birds eat half of the blue beetles and none of the gold, which they overlook. The beetles that survive will mate and lay eggs, and their young will grow up in the same meadow. Colour runs in families, so blue parents tend to have blue young and gold parents tend to have gold young.

The last lesson explained where new versions of a trait come from. This lesson asks what happens to them afterwards. It follows the beetles through one season and then a generation, counting how many of each colour there are and what share of the meadow each makes up, and it asks what that tells us and what it leaves open.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate how a variant's share of a population changes, and say what natural selection does and does not show.

recap.keyIdea: Heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common, and which variants do so depends on the environment. A frequency shift alone does not prove selection.

blocks.text: You turned beetle counts into frequencies and measured a fall of 15 percentage points and a rise of 30. You saw the same variant rise in one environment and fall in another, and you found that chance or migration can move a frequency without selection.

recap.nextHook: A population changes with what surrounds it: its food, its enemies and the weather. The next lesson widens the view from one species to a whole pond and follows who eats whom.

lessons.title: Follow the food

lead.text: The pond has a simple chain of feeding: the zooplankton eat the algae, and the small fish eat the zooplankton. Ecologists draw each of these links as an arrow that points from the food to the organism that eats it, so Algae → Zooplankton says that the zooplankton eat the algae. The arrow shows the way the food, and the energy in it, travels. Check the direction every time, because the arrow points towards the eater.

Real habitats are tangled. The heron eats small fish, and it also eats zooplankton directly, so two arrows end at the heron. A diagram that shows every feeding link in a habitat is a food web. The pond with all the living things in it and the surroundings they depend on is an ecosystem, and a food web is a map of the feeding in it. The arrows that end at an organism show its direct food sources.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the pond web. Look at the heron: arrows from Small fish and from Zooplankton both end there, so it has two direct food sources. The small fish have only one, because a single arrow reaches them.

lead.text: Count the arrows that end at the hawk.

Trace any route backwards along the arrows and you always end at the same sort of organism. The algae are not eating anything. They make their own food, using light, in the way a leaf cell does. An organism that makes its own food is called a producer. In a meadow the grass is the producer, and in the pond it is the algae.

Every other organism has to eat. Zooplankton, small fish and herons are consumers, which get their food by eating other organisms. The producers are the only ones that bring new food into the web, so every route starts at a producer, no matter how long it is. The heron's meal of small fish traces back to zooplankton, and the zooplankton to algae.

afterFigure.text: That makes the producers the foundation of the web. If they disappeared, every consumer would lose its food sooner or later, whatever the web looked like in between.

lead.text: Look for the organism that does not need to eat anything.

steps.headline: A change moves along the arrows

lead.text: Because the organisms are linked, a change in one passes to its neighbours. Look at the arrow Zooplankton → Small fish. If the small fish were removed, fewer zooplankton would be eaten, so the zooplankton would tend to increase. If the zooplankton fell in number instead, there would be less food for the small fish, so they would tend to decrease. A change travels in both directions along an arrow: towards the eaters, which lose food, and towards the food, which is eaten less.

Webs are never quite that simple. The heron has two sources of food, so when the zooplankton decline it still has small fish to eat. Many animals can switch to other foods. A diagram tells you which links exist and which way a change is likely to push. It does not tell you how big the effect will be.
Zooplankton eat algae. Use that arrow to decide which way the loss of the zooplankton pushes the algae.

steps.headline: Matter goes round, energy goes through

lead.text: The arrows leave out what happens when an organism dies. A dead heron does not stay as it is. Decomposers, mostly bacteria and fungi, feed on dead organisms and waste, and in doing so they return the matter in them to the soil and the water as simple substances. Producers take those substances up again and build them into new tissue. Some of the atoms in the algae today may once have been part of a heron. Matter goes round in a cycle.

Energy behaves differently. Producers capture it from light, and each step along an arrow passes some of it on, but at every step much of it escapes as heat that no organism can use again. Energy is never cycled back. It flows through the ecosystem, which is why a pond needs a steady supply of sunlight to keep going, while the matter in it can be used over and over.
Think about what happens to energy at each step along the arrows.
Think about what the arrows of a small web show and what they leave out.

lessons.orientation: Read feeding arrows and separate energy flow from recycled matter.

blocks.text: Stand at the edge of a pond on a still summer day. The water is faintly green, because it is full of microscopic algae. Among them swim tiny animals called zooplankton, which feed on the algae. Small fish swim through the zooplankton and eat them, and now and then a heron wades in and eats the small fish.

Everything in the pond is tied together by who eats whom. Suppose a disease sweeps through and kills most of the zooplankton. The loss will not stay with the zooplankton. It will spread to the animals that eat them, to the algae they eat and to the heron that wades in for fish, though it will not reach each of them in the same way.

This lesson learns to read a drawing of those links, with arrows that point from food to eater. It shows where every route in the drawing begins, how a change travels along the arrows and what the arrows leave out. By the end you can read the feeding in a habitat and say what moves round it and what only passes through.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the arrows of a food web and say which parts of an ecosystem are recycled and which are not.

recap.keyIdea: Arrows point from food to eater, and every route starts at a producer. Matter is recycled by decomposers, but energy flows through and disperses as heat.

blocks.text: You counted the direct food sources of a hawk and traced every route back to a producer. You followed a change along an arrow, and you saw why a diagram of links cannot predict an exact count.

recap.nextHook: Energy escapes as heat at every step along a route. The next lesson measures how much, and asks how much of a producer's energy is left by the time it reaches the top of the web.

lessons.title: Energy up the food chain

lead.text: Go back to the pond. The algae capture energy from sunlight. The zooplankton eat the algae, the small fish eat the zooplankton and the heron eats the small fish. Each of these is a separate step in who feeds on whom, and ecologists number the steps from the bottom. The algae are the producers and make up the first level. The zooplankton, which eat producers, make up the second. The small fish are the third level and the heron is the fourth. Each numbered step is called a trophic level.

The energy in food is measured in kilojoules, written kJ. Suppose the algae in a stretch of the pond hold 4000 kJ between them. That is the energy at the first level, and every animal above depends on it. The cow showed that an animal keeps only part of what it eats, so what we need to find out is how much of those 4000 kJ is still there once the zooplankton have eaten the algae.

An animal does not turn everything it eats into more animal. Some of the food is never eaten at all, such as the roots of a plant or the bones of a fish. Of the part that is eaten, some is not digested and leaves the body as waste. Most of what is digested is used up in living, which covers moving about and running the cells. All of that energy ends up as heat. Only what is left over is built into new body, and only new body is there for the next animal to eat.

So at every step along a chain, only a fraction of the energy at one level reaches the next. The percentage that passes up is the transfer efficiency. The cow built about a tenth of its food into new body, which is like a transfer efficiency of 10%. We will use 10% for the rest of this lesson unless a problem gives another figure.
This is the farmer's cow again. Set what it ate against what it gained.
Apply the transfer efficiency to the energy in the producers.

Now back to the 4000 kJ in the algae. At 10% transfer the zooplankton receive a tenth of it, which is 4000 × 0.1 = 400 kJ. The small fish do not receive a tenth of the original 4000 kJ. They eat the zooplankton, so they receive a tenth of what the zooplankton hold: 400 × 0.1 = 40 kJ. The heron receives a tenth of that, 40 × 0.1 = 4 kJ.

afterFigure.text: Each transfer starts from the energy that reached the level it leaves, so the 10% is applied again and again. Two transfers in a row leave 4000 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 40 kJ, which is one hundredth of what the chain began with. The figure stacks the levels with the widest at the bottom. That pyramid shape is what losing nine tenths at every step looks like.

lead.text: Work upwards from the producers, one step at a time.

The 10% we have used is a round number for working with, and it is not a law. Real efficiencies differ between ecosystems and between animals. Animals that keep their bodies warm use up more of their food as heat than animals that do not, and some foods are far easier to digest than others. For that reason a problem about energy transfer states the efficiency to use, and you use the one it gives.

afterFigure.text: The method does not change when the figure does. A higher efficiency lets more through at every step. With 3000 kJ in the producers, a 10% transfer passes on 300 kJ. A 20% transfer passes on 600 kJ, twice as much, because 0.2 is twice 0.1. After two steps the gap has widened. The 10% chain holds 30 kJ and the 20% chain holds 120 kJ, four times as much.

lead.text: Think about whether 10% is a measured fact or a figure a problem chooses.
This problem states a different efficiency. Use the figure it gives.

So far we have started at the bottom and gone up. Often the question runs the other way: how much energy must the lower levels hold to supply a given amount higher up. Each level receives a tenth of the level below, so the level below must hold ten times as much. To go backwards we undo the multiplication by dividing by the efficiency, written as a decimal, which is 0.10 for 10%.

Suppose the heron level is to receive 25 kJ. At 10% transfer the small fish must have held 25 ÷ 0.10 = 250 kJ, and for the small fish to hold that much the zooplankton must have held 250 ÷ 0.10 = 2500 kJ. Every step down multiplies the requirement by ten, so a small amount at the top needs a very large amount at the bottom. That is why food chains have so few levels, and why meat takes far more land to produce than plants do.
Now the question runs the other way. You are told what arrives and asked what had to be there.

lessons.orientation: Calculate trophic transfers using an explicit efficiency assumption.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with energy escaping as heat at every step along a route through a food web, and it left open how much escapes. A farm gives an easy place to start measuring.

A farmer feeds a cow 100 kg of grain. The cow eats it over several weeks, and in that time it gains 10 kg of body mass. Only a tenth of the grain has become cow. The rest was not built into the cow, and what happened to it is the subject of this lesson.

We will follow a quantity of energy up the pond's food chain, one feeding step at a time. At each step we will work out how much arrives. Then we will turn the chain round and find how much had to be there at the start to supply the top.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how much energy reaches each level of a food chain, and how much the bottom must supply.

recap.keyIdea: Only a stated fraction of the energy at one level passes to the next, so the energy shrinks at every step. Dividing by the same fraction works backwards.

blocks.text: You followed 4000 kJ up the pond from the algae and found 4 kJ left for the heron. You applied a stated 20% as well, and worked back from 300 kJ to the 3000 kJ the level below had to hold. The cow's 10 kg from 100 kg of grain was the same loss on a farm.

recap.nextHook: Energy limits how much life a place can feed. The next lesson takes one kind of living thing, a patch of water lilies on a pond, and watches what happens when nothing holds it back.

lessons.title: Limits to growth

lead.text: Follow the lily patch day by day. Today it covers 1 square metre. After one day it covers 2, after two days 4 and after three days 8. The patch grows by the same proportion every day, and that proportion is its growth rate. Doubling is a growth rate of 100% a day, because the patch gains as much area as it already had.

afterFigure.text: Look at what the numbers do. The patch adds 1 square metre on the first day, 2 on the second and 4 on the third. The growth rate stays the same, but the amount added gets bigger every day, because there is more patch to do the growing. The figure sets it beside a patch that simply gains 1 square metre a day, which falls behind. A doubling population creeps along at first and then takes off. It cannot go on for ever in a pond of fixed size, since the patch cannot cover more than the whole pond.

lead.text: Carry on doubling from where the figure stops.
The patch cannot go on doubling once the pond is nearly covered. Think about what the lilies need and how much of it there is for each leaf as the pond fills.

reveal.text: Compare your prediction with the figure. The patch still grows, but each day adds less than the day before.

lead.text: Look at the real pond's curve. For the first three days the lilies double, adding 1, 2 and 4 square metres. Over the next three days the patch adds 5, 4 and 2, a little less each time, and it levels off close to the pond's area of 20 square metres. The leaves are crowding one another for light and space, so new shoots find it harder to start and old leaves die more often. The same happens in every population. As numbers rise, each individual has less food, space or shelter to itself, and the competition lowers births or raises deaths, and often does both.

afterFigure.text: The size of population that a habitat can keep supporting is its carrying capacity. For the lilies in this pond it is set mostly by space, about 20 square metres. For deer it might be set by the winter food supply. A population that grows fast at first and then levels off near its carrying capacity traces an S-shaped curve, which biologists call logistic growth.

lead.text: Use the biologist's name for the size that the lily curve levels off near.

The curve is a record of numbers, and the numbers change for two main reasons. Individuals are born, and individuals die. To keep the count simple we use a closed population, one that nothing joins or leaves except through birth and death, so no animals arrive from elsewhere and none walk away. The difference between the births and the deaths in a period is the population's net change.

Take a closed population of 50, with 12 births and 7 deaths in a season. The net change is 12 − 7 = 5, so the population rises to 50 + 5 = 55. If deaths outnumbered births the net change would be negative and the population would fall. If births and deaths were equal, the population would stay the same size even though individuals were being born and dying all the time. That balance is what we see at the carrying capacity.
Count what the population gains and what it loses over one interval.
Find the net change first, then apply it to the starting size.

The carrying capacity of a habitat is not a fixed number. It depends on the resources the habitat offers, and those can change. Suppose half of the pond is filled in to make a path. The lilies now have only 10 square metres to spread across, and the same patch that once levelled off near 20 levels off near 10 instead. The carrying capacity of the pond for lilies has halved.

afterFigure.text: The same goes for other species. A habitat has a different carrying capacity for each species, because species need different things. Space for lilies says nothing about how many herons or fish the same pond can feed, since each depends on other resources. So a carrying capacity belongs to one species in one habitat under particular conditions, and when the conditions change, it changes with them.

lead.text: A population of grazing animals was near its limit when a drought cut the food supply.

steps.headline: What a smooth curve leaves out

lead.text: The S-shaped curve is a model: a simplified picture that keeps the main idea and leaves out the detail. It is useful because it shows why growth slows and roughly where it levels off. Real populations do not follow it exactly. Weather changes the food supply from year to year, disease can sweep through a crowded population, and chance decides which individuals happen to breed. A real count wobbles around the smooth line, and a population can overshoot its carrying capacity for a time before it falls back.

The curve explains the general pattern. To know what one particular population is doing you have to count it. A model that gets the shape right is doing its job, and it is asking too much of it to expect every rise and dip.

lessons.orientation: Compare proportional growth with resource-limited growth and changing carrying capacity.

blocks.text: The last lesson showed how little energy passes up a food chain, which means a pond can feed only so much life. This lesson asks what that limit does to a single kind of organism growing in it.

A pond covers 20 square metres. Today a single square metre of its surface is covered with water lilies, which float their leaves on the water and spread by sending out new shoots. Under good conditions the patch doubles its area every day. A group of one kind of living thing in one place is a population, and the lily patch is a population that is easy to follow, because its size is simply the area it covers.

For the first few days the patch hardly shows against the whole pond. Following it day by day shows how a population grows when nothing holds it back, what finally does hold it back, and how to keep count when individuals are born and die.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell unlimited growth from limited growth, and work out how births and deaths change a population.

recap.keyIdea: With nothing to hold it back a population grows faster each round, but limited resources slow it near the carrying capacity, and that limit changes with conditions.

blocks.text: You doubled a lily patch until it would have outgrown its pond, and watched the real patch level off near 20 square metres. You found a population's size from its births and deaths. You also saw half the pond filled in lower the limit to about 10 square metres.

recap.nextHook: Everything in these two lessons rested on numbers that someone measured. The next lesson asks how to test a claim with measurements, using two plants and a bag of fertiliser.

lessons.title: What counts as evidence

lead.text: A claim such as “fertiliser makes plants grow better” cannot be tested as it stands, because “better” can stand for different things to different people. To test it we choose an outcome, the thing we will measure to see whether the claim holds. A good outcome can be recorded with an instrument and written down as a number, and anyone repeating the test would measure it the same way.

Take a different claim as practice: “this lamp keeps seedlings healthier”. “Healthier” is a judgement, but the number of seedlings still alive after two weeks is a count, and the width of a leaf in millimetres is a measurement. Either would do, as long as we pick one before we start and keep to it. Choosing afterwards, whichever looks best, would let us find what we hoped to find. The gardener's claim is about growth, so her outcome has to be a number that records how much a plant has grown over a fixed time.
The gardener wants a measurement that records growth over a set time.

The gardener's two plants did not start at the same size, and that matters. Compare two seedlings, P and Q, over three weeks. P starts at 6 cm and finishes at 15 cm. Q starts at 10 cm and finishes at 17 cm. Q is taller at the end, but it was also taller at the start. A plant's starting measurement is its baseline, and what we want is the change from the baseline, which is the final height minus the baseline.
P grew 15 − 6 = 9 cm and Q grew 17 − 10 = 7 cm, so P grew more even though Q finished taller.

afterFigure.text: A final height mixes two things together: how big the plant already was and how much it grew. Subtracting the baseline removes the first and leaves the growth, which is what a fertiliser is supposed to change. For that reason we compare changes from baseline and not final sizes. The figure plots both seedlings week by week.

lead.text: Use the two plants from the start of the lesson. They began at different heights, just as P and Q did.

steps.headline: A control and a fair draw

lead.text: Growth on its own still proves little, because plants grow with or without fertiliser. We need something to compare the treated plants against. A control group is treated in every way the same except for the one thing being tested. In the gardener's test the control pots get plain water instead of fertiliser and have the same light and soil as the others. If the treated group grows 12 cm and the control 8 cm, the apparent effect of the fertiliser is the difference, 12 − 8 = 4 cm.

afterFigure.text: The groups also have to start out alike. If the gardener chooses by hand which pots get the fertiliser, she may put the pots nearest the window in the treated group without meaning to, and they would grow more because of the extra light. The remedy is random assignment: give each pot to a group by chance, with a coin or a shuffled pack of cards, so that differences in light, size and soil are spread over both groups.

lead.text: The pots are alike, and the gardener has to split them into two groups.
Compare the two groups over the same three weeks.

One treated pot and one control pot can still mislead, because individual plants vary. One seed may be weak, or one pot may drain badly. To see how much results vary, the test needs replicates: separate pots, each treated independently. Measuring the same pot ten times is not replication, since it only tells you more about that one pot.

With several pots we report the mean, which is the total of the growths divided by the number of pots. Three control pots that grow 5, 8 and 11 cm have a mean of (5 + 8 + 11) ÷ 3 = 8 cm. Three that grow 7, 8 and 9 cm also have a mean of 8 cm, but they tell a different story, because the first set is spread widely and the second sits close together. How far results are spread is their variability. A mean on its own can hide wide differences between pots, and a small gap between the treated and control means is hard to trust when the pots within each group differ a lot.
Share the total growth equally between the pots.

An experiment lets the experimenter decide which plants get the treatment. A survey does not. In a survey we go out and measure what is already there. Suppose surveyors visit 40 ponds and find that the ponds with more reeds also have more frogs. That is an association: the two rise and fall together. It is a fair reason to suspect that reeds help frogs, perhaps by giving them shelter, so it gives us a hypothesis worth testing.

afterFigure.text: An association does not show a cause by itself, because nobody assigned the reeds. Something else could lie behind both. In the figure the frogs rise with the reeds in sunny ponds and in shaded ones, yet the shaded ponds hold fewer frogs at every reed cover, so something other than reeds, such as light, matters too. To show that reeds cause the difference you would need an experiment that adds reeds to some ponds chosen at random and keeps the others as controls.

lead.text: Surveyors measure plants at many sites and find taller plants at the wetter ones. Nobody assigned the rainfall: this is an observation, not an experiment.

lessons.orientation: Design fair ecological comparisons and avoid turning correlation into an unsupported cause.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A gardener says that fertiliser makes plants grow taller, and she sets out to show it. One seedling gets fertiliser. It starts at 4 cm and after three weeks it stands at 19 cm. A second seedling gets none. It starts at 12 cm and after three weeks it stands at 22 cm. At the end the unfed plant is the taller one.

That looks bad for the fertiliser, but two plants cannot settle anything. A fair test has to decide what to measure and how to compare plants that start at different sizes. It also has to decide which plants get the treatment and how many plants to use.

The last two lessons used numbers that someone had to measure. This lesson follows the gardener's claim through those decisions one at a time, and ends with what a pattern seen in the wild can and cannot show.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge whether a plant experiment is fair, and say what an observed pattern can and cannot show.

recap.keyIdea: A fair test compares the change from baseline in a treated group and a control, assigns plants to groups by chance and uses independent replicates. A survey on its own shows an association and cannot show a cause.

blocks.text: You compared how much plants grew and set that against how tall they ended up, and you found a treated group 3 cm ahead of its control. You took the mean of three pots and saw why a mean needs its spread. You also saw why more frogs among more reeds does not prove that reeds are the cause.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. You have followed living things from the parts of a cell to the pond around a heron, and the habit of asking what was measured and how it was compared applies to every claim along the way.

questions.prompt: Both cells need food in and waste out. Name the structure around each cell that controls this exchange.
hints: Look at the outline of each cell.
Which layer acts as the doorkeeper, deciding what crosses?
Both cells share this structure, so it cannot be something only one of them has.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both cells exchange substances across a plasma membrane.

questions.onCorrect: The plasma membrane. Every cell has one, and it controls what enters and leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: A cell wall is an extra layer outside the boundary that some cells have. The boundary every cell has lies inside it.
You have the right kind of structure. Give its full name, as it appears on the first screen.
You have described where it is. The question asks for the structure's name.

questions.prompt: A bacterium has no nucleus. In which region of the cell does its DNA lie?
hints: Having no nucleus doesn't mean having no DNA.
Think of plans pinned to the wall of one open room, not locked in an office.
The region's name resembles the name of the compartment this cell lacks.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bacterial nucleoid holds DNA without a surrounding nuclear membrane.

questions.onCorrect: In the nucleoid. A bacterium has DNA, but no membrane wraps it.

misconceptions.feedback: Every cell has DNA. The bacterium just keeps it without a nuclear membrane.
A bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in a region with a different name.
That describes it fairly, but the question asks for the name of the region where the DNA gathers.

questions.prompt: Leaf cells capture light, but after dark they still need energy from fuel. Which organelle does that job?
hints: Which organelle works with the energy stored in fuel?
Does that organelle need light to do its job?
A root cell, which sits in the dark soil, has it too.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells have chloroplasts for light and mitochondria for energy from fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Mitochondria. A leaf cell has both organelles because it does both jobs.

misconceptions.feedback: Chloroplasts need light. The job here goes on in the dark.
Ribosomes build proteins. Look for the organelle that works on fuel.

questions.prompt: Name the structure outside a plant cell's membrane that helps the cell hold its shape.
hints: Think back to the water balloon inside a cardboard box.
Look at the outermost layer of the leaf cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cell wall gives external support; the membrane remains inside it.

questions.onCorrect: The cell wall. It props the cell up from outside and leaves the membrane in charge of exchange.

misconceptions.feedback: The membrane lies inside this layer. Name the structure outside it.

questions.prompt: A root cell is alive but has no chloroplasts. Which conclusion follows?
hints: Think about where roots are and what they do.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many plant cells, including root cells, have no chloroplasts and use sugars made elsewhere.

choices.label: It cannot be a plant cell
It cannot release energy from fuel

questions.onCorrect: Not every plant cell photosynthesises. Root cells use sugars made by the leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: Plant cells are defined by more than chloroplasts. Roots are plant tissue.
Releasing energy from fuel is the mitochondria's job, and root cells have those.

questions.prompt: Name the structure whose presence most directly shows that a cell is eukaryotic.
hints: Pick the distinctive structure, not one every cell shares.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane-bound nucleus distinguishes eukaryotic cells from bacterial cells.

questions.onCorrect: A nucleus. A plasma membrane is shared by all cells, so it can't tell the two types apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Bacteria have these too. Choose a structure bacteria lack.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes hold 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right, and solute can cross. In which direction is there net movement at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated? With equal volumes, compare the amounts.
Which side sends more particles across the membrane?
Net movement runs away from the crowded side.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side is more concentrated, so net solute movement is to the right.

questions.onCorrect: Left to right: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from the sparser side to the crowded one. Net movement goes the other way.
The two sides differ in concentration, so more particles cross one way than the other.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Keep the total solute constant.
Add the amounts on the two sides.
Divide the total between two equal volumes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 16 units divide equally: 16 ÷ 2 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8 each. Total solute stays constant, and equal volumes finish with equal amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That's both sides together. Share it between the two compartments.
That's the left side's starting amount. Some of it has moved across.

questions.prompt: 12 solute units start on the left and 4 on the right. The barrier blocks both solute and water. How many solute units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Check what can cross first.
If nothing can cross, can any amount change?
Each side keeps the amount it started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing can cross, so each side keeps its starting amount: 12 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 12. A barrier that blocks the solute leaves the amounts unchanged, whatever the difference in concentration.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need solute to cross, and this barrier blocks it.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left side.

questions.prompt: At equal concentration, 8 units are on each side. How many solute units are in the whole two-compartment system?
hints: Count both compartments.
There are eight units in each.
Add the two equal amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 8 = 16 units. Diffusion does not destroy solute.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Equilibrium means equal concentrations, not missing solute: the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That's one side. Count both compartments.

questions.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium, which statement is accurate?
hints: Separate no net change from no motion.

acceptedIdeas: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.

choices.label: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
All molecules move in one direction

questions.onCorrect: Particles keep crossing both ways at equal rates, so there is no net flow.

misconceptions.feedback: Particles keep moving. What stops is the net change in concentration.
One-way movement would keep changing the concentrations. At equilibrium the flows balance.

questions.prompt: A separate equal-volume system starts with 14 solute units on one side and 2 on the other. How many units must move net from the concentrated side to reach equilibrium?
hints: Find the equilibrium amount first.
The total is shared between two equal volumes.
Subtract the equilibrium amount from the starting amount on the crowded side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Find the equal share first, then see how far the crowded side must fall to reach it.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the amount each side ends with. How many had to move to get there?
That's the gap between the sides. Only half of the gap has to cross.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes hold 4 solute units on the left and 12 on the right, at equal pressure. Which side gains water at first?
hints: Compare the amounts of solute. The volumes are equal.
Which side holds less water in each litre?
Water drifts from where it is more crowded to where it is less crowded.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right side is more concentrated in solute, so it initially gains water.

questions.onCorrect: The right side, where the solute is more concentrated. Water moves towards more solute.

misconceptions.feedback: The left side has less solute. Water moves towards the more concentrated side, not away from it.

questions.prompt: As water enters the right compartment, what happens to its 12 solute units?
hints: The membrane's selectivity stays the same.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The membrane blocks solute; only its concentration changes.

questions.onCorrect: They stay. Only the water moves, so the solute is simply spread through a bigger volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute is never destroyed. It stays where it is.
The membrane blocks the solute, so it cannot cross.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration in units per volume?
hints: Use amount divided by volume.
Identify the amount and the volume in the question.
Divide the amount by the volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 units per volume.

questions.onCorrect: 6 per volume. Concentration is the amount of solute divided by the volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the amount by the volume. Concentration divides.
That's the amount alone. Divide by the volume.

questions.prompt: Why can the two volumes change while the total solute stays constant?
hints: Follow each substance separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the water distribution changes volumes without changing solute amount.

questions.onCorrect: Water moves and solute stays, so volumes change but each side's solute amount does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Solute stays solute. Only the water moves across.
Nothing creates solute here. Its amount is fixed on each side.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 8 units of trapped solute. Its volume increases from 1 to 2. By what factor is its concentration multiplied?
hints: Calculate the concentration before and after.
The solute amount is unchanged.
Divide the new concentration by the old one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration changes from 8 to 4, a factor of 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5. Doubling the volume halves the concentration when the solute amount is fixed.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a doubling. The volume grew, so the concentration fell.
That's the new concentration, not the factor between old and new.

questions.prompt: A plant cell wall builds an opposing pressure as water enters. Which prediction is justified?
hints: The real cell includes a force that the model leaves out.

acceptedIdeas: Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water movement depends on both solute concentration and pressure; the simple partition model omits this opposition.

choices.label: Water must keep entering without limit
Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry

questions.onCorrect: Pressure can reduce or stop net entry. Water movement depends on pressure as well as solute.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the wall. As the cell swells, the wall pushes back.
Nothing in the wall's pushing damages the membrane. The pressure just opposes more water entering.

questions.prompt: Name the energy barrier that an enzyme lowers.
hints: The ball has to be lifted over something before it can roll down.
Think of the height of the hill.
It is the energy a reaction needs before it can begin.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enzyme provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

questions.onCorrect: Activation energy. A lower barrier means more reactions get over it each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is not the barrier. Name the energy a reaction needs before it can start.

questions.prompt: Enzyme A's rates at 10, 25, 40 and 55°C are 2, 8, 12 and 3 units per minute. What is the highest rate measured, in units per minute?
hints: Compare all four measured rates.
Pick the largest of the four.
Use the plotted value, not a guess about other temperatures.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest of 2, 8, 12 and 3 is 12 units per minute, at 40°C.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units per minute, at 40°C. This is the best of the temperatures that were tested.

misconceptions.feedback: 40 is the temperature. The question asks for the rate.
That is the lowest rate, at the highest temperature.

questions.prompt: In an enzyme reaction every active site is busy, and adding more substrate no longer raises the rate. Which substance limits the rate?
hints: Ask which substance supplies the active sites.
Think of the ticket counters: what would add more counters?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fixed amount of enzyme limits how many substrate molecules can be processed at once.

questions.onCorrect: The enzyme. With every active site busy, extra substrate can't be processed any faster.

misconceptions.feedback: There is plenty of substrate. What is short is the thing that processes it.

questions.prompt: After 3 minutes, the matched enzyme sample has 27 product units and the control has 9. What is the difference?
hints: Compare the same elapsed time.
Read both amounts at three minutes.
Subtract the control from the enzyme sample.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 27 − 9 = 18 extra product units in this comparison.

questions.onCorrect: 18 extra units. A matched control lets you credit that difference to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two samples. A comparison subtracts.
That's the enzyme sample alone. Compare it with the control.

questions.prompt: A high-temperature treatment lowers one enzyme's activity. What is a plausible explanation?
hints: A protein's shape matters to its function.
Think about what heat does to the active site.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: High temperature can denature an enzyme and disrupt binding or catalysis.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at that temperature

questions.onCorrect: Its shape changed. A denatured active site no longer fits the substrate.

misconceptions.feedback: The activity fell, so this temperature is not the best one for this enzyme.
Past a point heat damages enzymes. Here the activity went down.

questions.prompt: Which experiment best tests an enzyme's effect?
hints: Separate the tested factor from other possible causes.
Which design changes one thing and keeps the rest the same?

acceptedIdeas: Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Holding other conditions constant isolates enzyme addition, while replication estimates variability.

choices.label: Change enzyme, temperature and pH together
Compare different organisms at unrelated times
Compare matched replicated samples that differ only in enzyme addition

questions.onCorrect: Change one thing and keep the rest matched, with repeats. Any difference then points to the enzyme.

misconceptions.feedback: With three changes at once, you can't tell which one caused the difference.
Different organisms and times add many other differences.

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies the carbon atoms in a leaf's newly made sugar.
hints: Rainwater has almost no carbon and light has no atoms.
Which gas carries carbon into a leaf?
It is the gas you breathe out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Light brings energy; the atoms for the sugar come from the gas.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Look for the gas that contains carbon.
Light is energy. It has no atoms to give.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in both glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms.
Each CO₂ contributes one carbon atom.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two glucose contain 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, so they need 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the carbon atoms in the sugar, because each came from one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is enough for one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, in what form is light energy stored?
hints: Think of the sugar the plant makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthesis captures some incoming light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

questions.onCorrect: Chemical energy, held in the bonds of sugar. Light itself adds no matter.

misconceptions.feedback: Some energy is lost as heat, but the energy that is captured is stored differently.
Carbon is matter. The question asks about the form of the energy.

questions.prompt: A leaf has a low supply of CO₂. Its photosynthetic rate is 8 at light level 60 and 8 at light level 80. By how much did the rate increase?
hints: Use the two rates given for the lower curve.
Subtract the first rate from the second.
What is the difference between two equal rates?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0. The curve is flat between those light levels.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The curve has plateaued, so something else, here the CO₂ supply, is limiting the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate itself, not the change in it.
That is the change in light level, not in the rate.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. Name the process, besides photosynthesis, that it uses to transfer energy from sugar.
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. Photosynthesis stores the energy, and respiration releases it for the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the process the question rules out. Name the other one.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: Read the number written in front of O₂.
Use that number of oxygen molecules for each glucose.
Multiply by three glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Six O₂ come with each glucose, so scale by the number of glucose molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are three.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the oxygen made for each one.

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: The name is three letters long.
It carries energy from where sugar is broken down to where work is done.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.onCorrect: ATP. Cells fill it with energy from fuel, then spend it on work.

misconceptions.feedback: Glucose is the fuel. Name the molecule that carries the transferred energy to the work.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down two glucose molecules using oxygen. How many CO₂ molecules does it produce?
hints: Each CO₂ contains one carbon.
Each glucose contains six carbons.
Count the carbon from two glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each carbon atom from the fuel ends up in one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the CO₂ from one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. It runs on stored fuel, so it carries on when the light goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Photosynthesis needs light, and there is none. Name the process that uses fuel.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of living organisms holds 20 units of oxygen at the start and 11 units after three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the starting and final oxygen amounts.
The final amount is lower.
Subtract the final amount from the starting amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 − 11 = 9 oxygen units.

questions.onCorrect: 9 units. Falling oxygen in a sealed jar is a sign that organisms are respiring.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was left. The question asks how much was used.
That adds the two amounts. Oxygen fell, so subtract.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon when a cell breaks the glucose down completely using oxygen?
hints: Follow the carbon-containing substances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

questions.onCorrect: It ends up in carbon dioxide. Atoms are conserved, and only the energy is transferred.

misconceptions.feedback: Matter doesn't turn into energy. The carbon atoms are still there afterwards.
Oxygen gas has no carbon in it. Look for a product that does.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: Compare moving air with chemistry in cells.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing can supply oxygen, but respiration is a set of chemical processes in cells.

choices.label: They are exactly the same reaction
Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air. Respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is a movement of air, not a reaction. Respiration is the reaction.
Plants and bacteria respire too, and they do not breathe.

questions.prompt: A new DNA base is placed opposite adenine (A). Give the name of the base that pairs with it.
hints: Each base has exactly one partner.
A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.
T stands for the base you need to name.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine in standard DNA base pairing.

questions.onCorrect: Thymine. A pairs with T, so the old strand decides which base comes next.

misconceptions.feedback: Those bases pair with each other, not with adenine.
Uracil is found in RNA. In DNA, adenine pairs with a different base.

questions.prompt: Write the partner bases beneath the strand 5′-AAGC-3′, from left to right.
hints: Pair one position at a time, keeping the same left-to-right order.
The first base is A, and A pairs with T.
Continue along the strand: A, G, then C.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The aligned partner is 3′-TTCG-5′; the two strands run in opposite directions.

questions.onCorrect: TTCG. Each base takes its partner in turn, and the partner strand runs the opposite way.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the order. Keep the partner bases in step with the strand above.
That copies the strand itself. Write each base's partner.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA molecule replicates once. How many double-stranded DNA molecules result?
hints: Separate strands serve as templates.
Each old strand receives a new partner.
Count the resulting paired molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One molecule is copied into two, each with one old and one new strand.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each old strand gets a new partner, so one molecule gives two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts strands. The question asks for double-stranded molecules.
The old strands each get a partner, which makes more than one molecule.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 chromosomes before copying. Immediately after copying, while sister chromatids remain joined, how many chromosomes does it have?
hints: DNA amount and chromosome number are different counts.
Joined sister chromatids belong to one replicated chromosome.
Keep the chromosome count unchanged at this stage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It still has four chromosomes; each now has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Copying doubles the DNA but not the number of chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the chromatids. Joined chromatids still make one chromosome each.
Copying does not halve anything. The count stays as it was.

questions.prompt: What does semiconservative replication keep in each resulting DNA molecule?
hints: Trace the two original strands separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each resulting molecule pairs an original template strand with a newly made strand.

questions.onCorrect: One original strand, paired with a new one. Each molecule is half old and half new.

misconceptions.feedback: The two original strands separate. Each ends up in a different molecule.
Every old strand is reused as a template, so each new molecule contains one.

questions.prompt: Six chromosomes each have two sister chromatids after copying. How many DNA molecules are present?
hints: Count both chromatids of each chromosome.
There are six replicated chromosomes.
Multiply the chromosomes by the chromatids in each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromatid contains one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each chromatid is one DNA molecule, and every chromosome now has two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts chromosomes. Each one now holds two DNA molecules.
That is the chromatids in one chromosome. There are more chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Name the nuclear division process used in ordinary tissue growth and repair.
hints: It keeps the starting chromosome number.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mitosis distributes copied chromosomes to daughter nuclei during regulated growth and repair.

questions.onCorrect: Mitosis. It shares copied chromosomes so each daughter nucleus gets a full set.

misconceptions.feedback: Meiosis makes sex cells and halves the chromosome number. Growth needs the full number kept.

questions.prompt: A cell has 6 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have after replication but before mitosis?
hints: Replication copies the DNA.
Each of the six chromosomes now has two chromatids.
Count the two DNA molecules in every replicated chromosome.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six replicated chromosomes have two chromatids each: 12 DNA molecules.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Every chromosome is copied, so it holds two DNA molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chromosomes. Each one now holds two DNA molecules.
That doubles twice. Replication copies each chromosome only once.

questions.prompt: A cell starts with 4 chromosomes and completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
hints: Think about the worksheet: each student got a full set.
Sister chromatids are separated equally.
Each daughter gets the same number the parent started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each daughter retains the original four chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Mitosis gives each daughter a full set, so the chromosome number stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Mitosis does not halve the number. Each daughter gets a full set.
That counts the chromatids before they separate. Each daughter gets one copy of each chromosome.

questions.prompt: One cell completes three ideal rounds of division, with every cell dividing in every round. How many cells result?
hints: Double once for each round.
After two rounds there are four cells.
Double the count a third time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each round doubles the number of cells, so three rounds make three doublings.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds two for each round. Each round doubles the count instead.
That counts the rounds. The question asks for the number of cells.

questions.prompt: Name the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome that separate during mitosis.
hints: Track the two copies made when a chromosome is replicated.
They stay joined until mitosis pulls them apart.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sister chromatids separate and become daughter chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They separate so each daughter nucleus gets one copy.

misconceptions.feedback: Homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes from two parents. The joined copies came from one.

questions.prompt: Does a normal body cell divide only because it is about to die?
hints: Separate regulated division from cell death.

acceptedIdeas: No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cell-cycle regulation responds to conditions and signals; imminent death is not the general cause.

choices.label: Yes, that is the defining trigger
No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
Yes, and the DNA need not be copied

questions.onCorrect: No. Division is regulated and happens when the body needs new cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Cells divide when growth or repair needs them to. Dying is not the trigger.
DNA is always copied first. Without a copy, a daughter would lack half its instructions.

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each pair contains two homologues.
There are three pairs.
Multiply the pairs by the chromosomes in each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three pairs contain 3 × 2 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Each homologous pair holds two chromosomes, so count them in twos.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Each pair holds two chromosomes.
Replication has not happened yet, so nothing has been doubled.

questions.prompt: Name the paired chromosomes that are pulled apart in meiosis I.
hints: The pair holds matching chromosomes from the two sets.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.onCorrect: Homologous chromosomes. Pulling them apart is what halves the chromosome number.

misconceptions.feedback: Sister chromatids stay joined in meiosis I. They part in the second division.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Meiosis reduces two chromosome sets to one.
The starting cell has two homologous pairs.
Take one chromosome from each pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each final cell holds one chromosome from each pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the starting number. Each final cell has only one set.
A final cell has one from each pair, and there are two pairs.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 3 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Two haploid sets combine to restore a diploid cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one gamete's contribution. Fertilisation brings two together.
Each gamete supplies three, so add only those two amounts.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
Between the divisions, the DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The second division separates the copies already made, so the amount of DNA halves again.

misconceptions.feedback: That round happens once, before meiosis I. None happens between the divisions.
Each division is a separation, not a copying.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Chromosome counts can match while the combinations differ.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Each parent has no genetic variation
Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis

questions.onCorrect: Chromosomes assort and swap segments, so every gamete carries a different mix.

misconceptions.feedback: Parents carry different versions of genes on their chromosomes.
Gametes differ from one another because of how meiosis shuffles chromosomes.

questions.prompt: What term describes the Aa parent, which carries two different alleles at this gene?
hints: The term contrasts with homozygous.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa is heterozygous; its two different alleles can separate into gametes.

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygous. Two different alleles, so it can pass on either one.

misconceptions.feedback: Homozygous means both alleles are the same. Aa has two different ones.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to have genotype aa?
hints: Look at all four pairings.
Count the aa boxes.
Convert the fraction of boxes to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of four equally likely pairings is aa: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

questions.onCorrect: 25%. One box in four is aa, and each box is equally likely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of Aa. aa fills only one box.
That is the chance of the dominant phenotype. The question asks about genotype aa.

questions.prompt: With A completely dominant, which genotypes have the dominant phenotype?
hints: Keep genotype letters separate from the expressed trait.

acceptedIdeas: Two dominant alleles, or one of each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One A allele is enough for the dominant phenotype in this model.

choices.label: Two dominant alleles, or one of each

questions.onCorrect: AA and Aa both. One dominant allele is enough to show the dominant trait.

misconceptions.feedback: Two recessive alleles give the recessive trait. Look for the genotypes that hide it.
Every organism has two alleles at the gene, so one of the options must apply.

questions.prompt: Four offspring are produced from Aa × Aa. Which statement is justified?
hints: A probability describes the long-run pattern.

acceptedIdeas: Each has a 25% chance of being aa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Independent random outcomes do not enforce a fixed family quota.

choices.label: Each has a 25% chance of being aa

questions.onCorrect: Each offspring has the same chance. Four children need not include exactly one aa.

misconceptions.feedback: Each birth is independent. A family can have none, or several.
A quarter of pairings are aa, so each child has a chance of it.

questions.prompt: For Aa × aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to show the recessive phenotype?
hints: The aa parent always passes on a.
The Aa parent passes on a half the time.
Convert that fraction to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two of four equally likely pairings are aa: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. Only aa shows the recessive trait, and half the offspring are aa.

misconceptions.feedback: The Aa parent passes on A half the time, and those offspring show the dominant trait.
That is the chance for Aa × Aa. This cross has an aa parent, which changes the odds.

questions.prompt: In this model, Aa and AA share a phenotype. What term describes A relative to a?
hints: Name how the allele is expressed, not how common it is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is dominant in this genotype-to-phenotype relationship; that does not establish its frequency or fitness effect.

questions.onCorrect: Dominant. It shows whenever it is present, but that says nothing about how common it is.

misconceptions.feedback: The recessive allele is the one that shows only with two copies. A shows with one.
Dominance is about expression. It does not mean the allele is common.

questions.prompt: ATCG changes to ATGG without changing length. Name this type of single-base change.
hints: No base was inserted or removed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The third base was substituted: C became G.

questions.onCorrect: A substitution. One base was swapped for another, so the length stayed the same.

misconceptions.feedback: An insertion or deletion would change the length. Here the length stayed the same.

questions.prompt: Compare AATG with AACG. How many displayed positions differ?
hints: Align the sequences from the left.
Compare each pair of letters in turn.
Count the mismatches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only position three differs: T became C.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Compare position by position and count only the mismatches.

misconceptions.feedback: The sequences are not identical. Check each pair of letters.
Only one pair of letters disagrees. Check each pair again.

questions.prompt: Name the reproductive cell type that can carry a DNA mutation directly into an offspring at fertilisation.
hints: Ordinary skin cells do not contribute DNA at fertilisation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contributing gamete can carry a DNA variant into the offspring.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete. Only the egg and sperm pass DNA to the next generation.

misconceptions.feedback: Body cells do not take part in fertilisation. Name the cell that does.

questions.prompt: A useful variant becomes more frequent after an environmental change. Which explanation avoids a directed-mutation error?
hints: Separate where a variant comes from from how it spreads.

acceptedIdeas: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection can change the frequency of existing variants; need does not direct a specific helpful mutation.

choices.label: Organisms created exactly the mutation they needed
Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
Every individual rewrote its DNA on purpose

questions.onCorrect: Variants were already there. Those that helped their carriers leave more offspring became more common.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations are not made to order. The variant was already present or arose by chance.
Individuals cannot rewrite their DNA to meet a need.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a phenotype.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: Its biological effect needs additional evidence

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences TCGATA and TCAACA. How many positions differ?
hints: Keep both sequences aligned.
Check each of the six positions in turn.
Count the mismatched pairs only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 3 and 5 differ; the other four agree.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Positions 3 and 5 disagree, so two bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the positions that differ.

questions.prompt: 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant. What percentage is blue?
hints: Use the blue count divided by the total.
The total is the blue and the other colour together.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 25%. A frequency is the variant's count divided by the whole population.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Divide it by the whole population and convert to a percentage.
That is the share that is not blue.

questions.prompt: Heritable variants consistently leave different numbers of reproducing descendants. Name the evolutionary process described.
hints: The difference is consistent, unlike random sampling.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Natural selection changes frequencies through differences in reproductive success associated with heritable traits.

questions.onCorrect: Natural selection. Heritable differences in offspring numbers shift the frequencies.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutation creates new variants. This is the sorting of variants that already exist.
The question says the difference is consistent and tied to the variant, which is not chance.

questions.prompt: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?
hints: Calculate each frequency using the total of 50.
Convert each fraction to a percentage.
Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency rises from 30% to 60%, a 30-point increase.

questions.onCorrect: 30 points. Work out both frequencies, then subtract.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in count. The question asks for the rise in frequency.
That is the later frequency, not the rise.

questions.prompt: A small population's variant frequency changes. Is selection the only possible cause?
hints: A pattern can have more than one cause.

acceptedIdeas: No, chance and migration can also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several evolutionary processes can change frequency; causal evidence is needed.

choices.label: Yes, every frequency shift proves selection
No, chance and migration can also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Chance and migration also shift frequencies, so a shift alone does not show selection.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift only shows that a frequency changed. It does not say why.
Populations change all the time, which is why the question matters.

questions.prompt: A once-useful trait becomes disadvantageous after a habitat change. Is this compatible with natural selection?
hints: Fitness depends on context.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection depends on how traits affect reproduction in the current environment.

choices.label: No, useful traits are always useful
Only if the organism chooses it
Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment

questions.onCorrect: Yes. A trait's advantage depends on the environment, so a new habitat can reverse it.

misconceptions.feedback: Usefulness depends on the environment, so a trait can stop helping.
Organisms do not choose the effect of their traits. The environment sets it.

questions.prompt: A later population has 18 blue and 42 gold organisms. What percentage is blue?
hints: Find the total population.
Divide the blue count by the total.
Convert the result to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 30%. Blue is 18 of 60, so its share is a little under a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the blue count. Divide it by the whole population.
That is the share that is gold.

questions.prompt: What does the arrow Grass → Grasshopper mean?
hints: Follow the direction of matter and energy transfer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrows run from food to consumer.

choices.label: Grass turns directly into a hawk

questions.onCorrect: The grasshopper eats the grass. An arrow runs from the food to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the arrow backwards. It points to whichever organism is doing the eating.
An arrow shows eating, not turning into another organism.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: Which organism makes its own food from light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae build organic matter using light; the other organisms consume other organisms.

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They build their own food, so all the other organisms depend on them.

misconceptions.feedback: Animals eat other organisms. The producer is the one that makes its own food.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web, a hawk eats mice and frogs. Frogs eat grasshoppers, which eat grass. How many direct food sources does the hawk have?
hints: Count the arrows ending at the hawk.
Do not count indirect food sources.
Ignore the grass and the grasshopper: the hawk does not eat them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two arrows enter the hawk: one from mouse and one from frog.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count only the arrows that end at the hawk.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every organism in the web. Count only those the hawk eats directly.
That includes organisms further down the routes. Count only direct links.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through ecosystems and becomes less available for further biological work. In what form does much of it disperse?
hints: Think about metabolic energy that is not passed into new biomass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy disperses as heat; atoms can be recycled through environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Energy flows through and spreads out as heat, so ecosystems need a steady input.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are recycled. Energy is not, and it spreads out in another form.

questions.prompt: In a meadow food web the number of mice goes down. Can the diagram give an exact future number of hawks?
hints: Check what the arrows actually show.

acceptedIdeas: No, other food sources and conditions also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A feeding web shows relationships, not a complete quantitative population model.

choices.label: Yes, arrows specify exact population changes
No, other food sources and conditions also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Arrows show who eats whom, not how many. Other food and conditions matter too.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show feeding links only. They give no numbers.
The hawk also eats frogs, so losing mice does not remove its food entirely.

questions.prompt: A pond web is a chain of algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron, plus one extra link where the heron also eats zooplankton directly. How many feeding links does the web have in total?
hints: Count the links in the chain first.
A chain of four organisms has one fewer link than organisms.
Add the extra link.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain has 3 links, and the extra link makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Count the links in the chain, then add the shortcut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chain alone. Add the extra link.
That is one more than the web has. A chain of four organisms has three links.

questions.prompt: The producers in a habitat hold 1000 kJ of energy. At an assumed transfer efficiency of 10%, how many kJ reach the next level?
hints: Convert the percentage to a decimal fraction.
Apply the fraction to the producers' energy.
Multiply the producers' energy by one tenth.
questions.onCorrect: 100 kJ. A 10% transfer passes on one tenth of the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy that does not pass on. The question asks how much reaches the next level.
That multiplies by ten. A percentage below a hundred makes the amount smaller.

questions.prompt: The producers hold 2000 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 3?
hints: Level 3 is two steps above the producers.
Apply 10% at each step.
Take one tenth of the energy left after the first step.
questions.onCorrect: 20 kJ. Two 10% steps leave 1% of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 2. One more transfer is needed to reach level 3.
That subtracts a tenth instead of passing on a tenth.

questions.prompt: With 5000 kJ at producers and a 20% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 2?
hints: Use the stated efficiency.
A fifth is the same as 20%.
Take one fifth of the producers' energy.
questions.onCorrect: 1000 kJ. A stated 20% passes on twice as much as 10% would from the same start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10% of the producers' energy. This problem states 20%.
That is the energy that does not pass on. Level 2 receives the share that does.

questions.prompt: A consumer level is to receive 300 kJ. At an assumed 10% transfer, how many kJ must the level below hold?
hints: Work backward through the transfer.
The required output is one tenth of the input.
Divide the required energy by the efficiency as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: 3000 kJ. Working backwards means dividing by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the efficiency, which goes forwards. Work backwards by dividing.
That adds a tenth of the amount on. Undoing a transfer of one tenth takes a division.

questions.prompt: Does every real food web transfer exactly 10% between levels?
hints: Separate a modelling assumption from a measured law.

acceptedIdeas: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ten-percent value is a useful stated approximation, not an exact universal constant.

choices.label: No, efficiency varies and must be specified or measured
No, energy is always fully transferred

questions.onCorrect: No. Efficiency varies between systems, so a problem states the value to use.

misconceptions.feedback: Measured efficiencies differ between ecosystems. 10% is a stated assumption.
Much of the energy is used by the organisms or disperses as heat.

questions.prompt: A fourth level is three steps above producers. From 8000 kJ with an assumed 10% transfer at each step, how many kJ reach level 4?
hints: Count the number of transfers.
Apply the efficiency once for each transfer.
Track the sequence step by step.
questions.onCorrect: 8 kJ. Three transfers at 10% leave one thousandth of the starting energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy at level 3. One more transfer is needed.
That is the energy at level 2. Two more transfers are needed.

questions.prompt: A population starts at 10 and doubles each round. What is it after three rounds?
hints: Double once per round.
After two rounds there are 40.
Double once more.
questions.onCorrect: 80. Each round doubles the last, so the increases grow larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 each round. Each round doubles instead.
That is the count after only two rounds.

questions.prompt: A population grows quickly at first and then levels off. What is the name for the size of population that its habitat can keep supporting?
hints: Competition for resources lowers net growth near this level.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity reflects the population supported by those conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Carrying capacity. Growth levels off near the size the habitat can support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are rates. The question asks for the size the habitat can support.

questions.prompt: A closed population has 12 births and 12 deaths in one interval. What is its net change?
hints: Gains add and losses subtract.
There is no migration in this closed population.
Subtract the deaths from the births.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 12 = 0, although individuals were born and died.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Births and deaths balance, so the size is steady even though individuals come and go.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births and deaths together. Deaths take away from the population.
That is the births alone. Take the deaths away.

questions.prompt: After a drought reduces the food supply, what may happen to the carrying capacity?
hints: The environment has changed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity depends on environmental resources and conditions.

choices.label: It becomes the same for every species

questions.onCorrect: It can decrease. Carrying capacity depends on conditions, so it is not a fixed number.

misconceptions.feedback: It depends on resources, and a drought changes them.
Each species needs different resources, so each has its own limit.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 70, with 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its final size?
hints: Start with the original population.
Add the births.
Subtract the deaths.
questions.onCorrect: 77. Net change is births minus deaths, added to the starting size.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the deaths. Subtract them.
That swaps the two: it subtracts the births and adds the deaths.

questions.prompt: Does a smooth logistic curve predict every fluctuation in a wild population?
hints: Identify the processes the model omits.

acceptedIdeas: No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve is a simplified model; real populations can fluctuate or overshoot.

choices.label: Only for populations above one million
No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures
